順天府鄉試錄序

聖天子嗣統紀元之年，秋八月，天下當大比士於鄉。順天府府尹臣紹儒、府丞臣守庭，職在提調，以例請。上命右諭德臣士美、右中允臣四維為考試官。臣士美方代草制言，兼纂修，祗役于舘，聞命兢惕。臣伏自思念：一介草茅，經術譾陋，曩歲己未獲對大廷，蒙先帝采擇，賜臣及第，旋授史秩，迄茲竊祿
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the year when the sagely Son of Heaven succeeded to the imperial line and inaugurated his reign era, candidates throughout the realm were due to undergo the triennial Provincial Examination. Your servants Shaoru, Prefect of Shuntian, and Shouting, Vice Prefect, whose duties included serving as Proctors, submitted a request in accordance with precedent. His Majesty appointed your servants Shimei, Right Mentor, and Siwei, Right Rectifier, as Examiners. I, your servant Shimei, was then drafting imperial pronouncements and concurrently engaged in compilation, respectfully carrying out my duties at the Hanlin Academy. On receiving the command, I felt apprehension and awe. I humbly reflected: a mere man of humble origins, with shallow learning in the Classics, I had been granted the opportunity in the jiwei year [1559] to answer questions at the imperial court. The late emperor graciously selected me and bestowed upon me a passing rank in the Palace Examination. Soon afterward, I was appointed to a historiographical post; ever since, I have undeservedly drawn an official stipend…

九年，罔效尺寸，惴惴焉惟瘝曠是懼。頃緣校錄《大典》，荷蒙皇上擢拔今官，至是又幸叨任使。深惟先帝之殊知，仰戴聖皇之隆遇，雖殫竭捐糜，何裨高厚？所藉手以答聖恩萬分之一者，惟得士也。
臣等以七日巳丑陛辭入院，廼率簾以內諸臣，矢公矢慎，更相飭戒。合六館諸曹暨提學御史臣龐尚鵬所選士三千八百五十有竒，三
translation_en:
…for nine years, without rendering even the slightest service, trembling in fear only of neglecting my duties. Recently, for my work collating and transcribing the Great Compendium, I received His Majesty’s gracious promotion to my present office; now I have again been fortunate enough to be entrusted with this commission. Reflecting deeply upon the late emperor’s exceptional recognition of me, and gratefully acknowledging the reigning emperor’s generous favor, I ask: even if I exhausted my strength and sacrificed my life, what could I contribute to such heaven-high, earth-deep bounty? The only means by which I might repay even one ten-thousandth of the imperial grace is to find worthy men.
On the seventh day, designated sichou 巳丑 [?], we, your servants, took leave of Your Majesty and entered the examination compound. We then led all the officials within the inner curtain in pledging impartiality and care, admonishing and cautioning one another. Those from the six colleges and the various offices, together with the candidates selected by your servant Pang Shangpeng, Censor supervising education, numbered somewhat more than 3,850. In three …

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
試之遵
制額拔百三十有五人並錄其
文以
獻臣士美謹序諸首曰休哉茲
我
皇上龍飛第一舉也士人之際此
也其千載一時哉乾之九五
飛龍在天利見大人文言申
之曰雲從龍風從虎聖人作
而萬物覩誠以俊士俟明主
以顯其德聖主待賢臣而弘
功業感召之機理有固然也
今
天子乘龍御極百度咸貞

文以

我
皇上龍飛第一舉也士人之際比

punctuated: 試之，遵制額拔百三十有五人，並錄其文以獻。臣士美謹序諸首曰：「休哉！茲我皇上龍飛第一舉也。士人之際此也，其千載一時哉！《乾》之九五：『飛龍在天，利見大人。』《文言》申之曰：『雲從龍，風從虎，聖人作而萬物覩。』誠以俊士俟明主以顯其德，聖主待賢臣而弘功業，感召之機，理有固然也。今天子乘龍御極，百度咸貞，
translation_en:
…examined them and, following the prescribed quota, selected 135 men, also recording their essays for presentation to the throne. Your servant Shimei respectfully places this preface at the beginning, saying:

“How auspicious! This is the first Provincial Examination since our emperor’s accession, his ascent as a dragon. For scholars to encounter such a moment—is this not an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years? The fifth yang line of Qian, ‘The Creative,’ reads: ‘The flying dragon is in heaven; it is beneficial to see the great man.’ The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) elaborates: ‘Clouds follow the dragon; winds follow the tiger. The sage arises, and all beings behold him.’ Indeed, outstanding scholars await an enlightened ruler through whom to manifest their virtue, while a sage ruler awaits worthy ministers through whom to enlarge his achievements. Such mutual attraction and response follow an inherent principle.

“Now the Son of Heaven has mounted the dragon and ascended the throne, and all institutions have been set right…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大號初頒遐邇敬應黎獻共臣
雖噓氣成雲不是速矣臣嘗
列在交戟之内見徼外八蠻
之長羶裘卉服之酋罔弗稽
首北面重譯貢琛者矧巖穴
之士思躡風雲之會者乎矧
都人士之首善而豹變者乎
===
其文之蔚當無疑矣因是繹
思昔我
太祖再造區夏即位之八年
命御史臺官選國子生分教北
方十四年
詔以五經四書頒降之我
成祖奠鼎燕都又作新而文明之

思昔我
太祖再造區夏即位之八年
命御史臺官選國子生分教北
方十四年
詔以五經四書頒降之我

punctuated: 大號初頒，遐邇敬應，黎獻共臣。雖噓氣成雲，不是速矣。臣嘗列在交戟之内，見徼外八蠻之長、羶裘卉服之酋，罔弗稽首北面，重譯貢琛者。矧巖穴之士思躡風雲之會者乎？矧都人士之首善而豹變者乎？其文之蔚，當無疑矣。因是繹思，昔我太祖再造區夏，即位之八年，命御史臺官選國子生分教北方。十四年，詔以五經四書頒降之。我成祖奠鼎燕都，又作新而文明之。
translation_en:
…The great proclamation has just been issued, and those far and near respond reverently; the worthy men among the people all acknowledge themselves as subjects. Even breathing out clouds would not be so swift [?]. Your servant once stood within the palace’s crossed halberds and saw the chiefs of the eight barbarian peoples beyond the frontier, leaders clad in sheepskins and garments of plant fiber: all bowed their heads to the ground, faced north as subjects, and presented precious tribute through successive interpreters. How much more, then, would scholars dwelling in secluded caves wish to seize this auspicious meeting of wind and cloud? And how much more would the scholars of the capital, foremost in goodness, transform themselves like leopards acquiring their patterned coats? There can be no doubt that their literary accomplishments will flourish.
This leads me to reflect further. Formerly, our Taizu reestablished the Chinese realm. In the eighth year after his accession, he ordered officials of the Censorate to select students of the Directorate of Education and dispatch them to teach throughout the north. In the fourteenth year, he decreed that the Five Classics and Four Books be distributed there. Our Chengzu established the seat of the dynasty at the capital of Yan and further renewed and cultivated its civilization.…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
迨
仁宗與侍臣論取士之例亦云長
才大器多出北方我
祖宗之注意北學也何肫切哉且
雅之詩曰思皇多士生此王
國王國克生維周之楨又古
稱慷慨之士燕趙之產居多
===
順天
畿邑即周之王國也於古為燕
趙地當必有楨
國之英慷慨之士如我
仁宗所云長才大器者出於其間
以應
聖作物覩之期以鳴

punctuated: 迨仁宗與侍臣論取士之例，亦云：「長才大器多出北方。」我祖宗之注意北學也，何肫切哉！且雅之詩曰：「思皇多士，生此王國。王國克生，維周之楨。」又古稱慷慨之士，燕趙之產居多。順天畿邑，即周之王國也，於古為燕趙地，當必有楨國之英、慷慨之士，如我仁宗所云長才大器者，出於其間，以應聖作物覩之期，以鳴
translation_en: When Emperor Renzong discussed the procedures for selecting officials with his attendant ministers, he too said: “Men of outstanding talent and great capacity mostly come from the north.” How deeply and earnestly our imperial ancestors attended to learning in the north! Moreover, a poem in the Odes of the Book of Poetry says: “Glorious are the many worthy men, born in this royal realm. The royal realm can indeed bring them forth: they are the pillars of Zhou.” It has also been said since antiquity that men of generous spirit and high resolve are most often natives of Yan and Zhao. Shuntian, the metropolitan territory, is the counterpart of Zhou’s royal realm; in antiquity it was the land of Yan and Zhao. Surely there must arise among its people outstanding men who are pillars of the state, men of generous spirit and high resolve—those of outstanding talent and great capacity of whom our Emperor Renzong spoke—to answer this moment when the sage arises and all beings behold him, and to proclaim…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
文治維新之盛也已臣承乏品
隲其文見其闡明道術根極
理要有其言章章者必曰此
都人士之豹變而文蔚者也
不然必游於都會者也錄之
見其敷陳經濟切中事情有
其言秩秩者必曰此慷慨之
===
士燕趙之產也不然則游於
燕趙者也錄之見其天才大
雅卓越不羣有洋洋颯颯者
必曰此長才大器者也亟錄
之其鈎棘者刻削者曼衍而
無當者弗錄因諗諸同事者
曰郁乎都人士之文也斌斌

punctuated: 文治維新之盛也已。臣承乏品隲其文，見其闡明道術、根極理要，有其言章章者，必曰：「此都人士之豹變而文蔚者也，不然必游於都會者也。」錄之。見其敷陳經濟、切中事情，有其言秩秩者，必曰：「此慷慨之士，燕趙之產也，不然則游於燕趙者也。」錄之。見其天才大雅、卓越不羣，有洋洋颯颯者，必曰：「此長才大器者也。」亟錄之。其鈎棘者、刻削者、曼衍而無當者，弗錄。因諗諸同事者曰：「郁乎都人士之文也！斌斌
translation_en: …the flourishing renewal of civil governance. Your servant, serving for want of someone better qualified, assessed their writings. Whenever I saw an essay that elucidated the Way and its teachings, probed the essentials of principle to their roots, and expressed its meaning with conspicuous clarity, I invariably said: “This is a man of the capital whose transformation, like a leopard’s, reveals richly patterned refinement; otherwise, he must be someone who has spent time in the capital.” I selected it. Whenever I saw an essay that expounded the arts of governance, addressed actual circumstances precisely, and expressed its ideas in orderly fashion, I invariably said: “This is a spirited and high-minded man, a native of Yan and Zhao; otherwise, he must have spent time in Yan and Zhao.” I selected it. Whenever I saw natural talent and lofty elegance, outstanding and beyond the common run, with an expansive and vigorous flow, I invariably said: “Here is a man of exceptional talent and great capacity.” I selected it at once. Writings that were tangled and thorny, excessively chiseled, or rambling and wide of the mark, I did not select. I then addressed my colleagues, saying: “How splendid is the literary refinement of the men of the capital! So richly balanced in substance and refinement…”

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盛於斯為盛哉非我
聖天子自新新民之會何以有此
哉既又惟之以主司之所取
於多士者文也多士異日之
所施樹者行也聽言可信行
與諸士行將□
大對布有位矣果行如其言終
===
如其始亮工熙載濟濟師師
使世人稱曰某良士某良士
隆慶丁卯
京闈所舉也龍興致雲得人之
盛果出尋常遠甚斯無負遭
際之隆而有光於
至治之會矣可亦可幸以逭責矣
alt_text:
徒於斯其爲盛哉非我
聖天子自新新民之會何以有此
哉既又惟之以主司之所取
於多士者文也多士異日之
所施樹者行也聽言可信行
與諸士行將來
大對布有位矣果行如其言終
如其始亮工熙載濟濟師師
使世人稱曰某良士某良士
===
隆慶丁卯
京闈所舉也龍興致雲得人之
盛果出尋常遠甚斯無負遭
際之隆而有光於
上治之會矣司亦可幸以逭責矣
punctuated: 盛於斯為盛哉！非我聖天子自新新民之會，何以有此哉？既又惟之，以主司之所取於多士者，文也；多士異日之所施樹者，行也。聽言可信行與？諸士行將□大對，布有位矣。果行如其言，終如其始，亮工熙載，濟濟師師，使世人稱曰：「某良士，某良士，隆慶丁卯京闈所舉也。」龍興致雲，得人之盛，果出尋常遠甚。斯無負遭際之隆，而有光於至治之會矣。可亦可幸以逭責矣。
translation_en:
…flourishing here—how splendid indeed! Were this not a time when our sage Son of Heaven renews himself and renews the people, how could this have come about?

Then I reflected further: what we examiners select from the many candidates is their writing; what these candidates will put into practice and accomplish in days to come is their conduct. Can hearing their words warrant confidence in their conduct? You gentlemen will soon □ present your great responses at the Palace Examination and take your places in office. If your conduct indeed matches your words, and your endings match your beginnings, you will faithfully discharge your duties and bring your undertakings to fruition, an impressive company taking one another as models. Then people throughout the realm will say: “This worthy man, and that worthy man, were recommended by the capital’s Provincial Examination in the dingmao year of Longqing [1567].” As the dragon rises and draws the clouds to it, the abundance of talent obtained will indeed far surpass the ordinary. Thus you will not betray the extraordinary good fortune of your encounter with this age, but will add lustre to this time of consummate governance. I too [?] may count myself fortunate to escape blame.

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
廼或靜言庸違有初鮮終奪
志於紛華黷道於貨賄罔恤
於蒸黎以賢入者以不肖黜
焉無論爲賢書玷貽主司羞
卽
祖宗之所注意何如
聖主作之所感召何如而忍負之耶
===
諸士固萬不至是臣於其始
進也不厭相與忠告云是役
也同考則進士臣應薦臣應
同知臣漢推官臣楨知州臣
訓知縣臣綵教諭臣模臣希
周臣津監試則御史臣儒臣
聯芳奉例增設則御史臣馬

punctuated:
廼或靜言庸違，有初鮮終，奪志於紛華，黷道於貨賄，罔恤於蒸黎，以賢入者以不肖黜焉。無論爲賢書玷、貽主司羞，卽祖宗之所注意何如，聖主作之所感召何如，而忍負之耶？
諸士固萬不至是，臣於其始進也，不厭相與忠告云。是役也，同考則進士臣應薦、臣應，同知臣漢，推官臣楨，知州臣訓，知縣臣綵，教諭臣模、臣希周、臣津。監試則御史臣儒、臣聯芳，奉例增設則御史臣馬
translation_en:
Yet should any speak fine words in repose but act contrary to them, begin well but seldom persevere to the end, let glittering luxuries divert their resolve, sully the Way through wealth and bribes, and show no concern for the common people, those admitted as worthy would be dismissed as unworthy. Quite apart from blemishing the roll of worthies and bringing shame upon the examiners, how great was the concern bestowed by the imperial ancestors, and how profound the inspiration imparted by the sage sovereign’s encouragement! Could they bear to betray it?
Surely none of these gentlemen would ever sink to this. Nevertheless, as they first enter official life, I, your servant, do not tire of offering them earnest counsel. For this examination, the Associate Examiners were your servants Yingjian and Ying, metropolitan graduates (jinshi); Han, a Vice Prefect; Zhen, a Prefectural Judge; Xun, a Department Magistrate; Cai, a District Magistrate; and Mo, Xizhou, and Jin, Instructors. Oversight of the examination was entrusted to your servants Ru and Lianfang, Censors. An additional appointment made pursuant to the regulations was that of the Censor, your servant Ma…

四書

周之冕樂則韶舞放鄭聲遠佞人鄭聲
淫佞人殆
知斯三者則知所以修身知所以修身則
知所以治人知所以治人則知所以治
天下國家矣
是集義所生者非義襲而取之也行有不
===
慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未嘗知義
以其外之也
易

求口實觀其自養也

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

顏淵問爲邦。子曰：「行夏之時，乘殷之輅，服周之冕，樂則韶舞。放鄭聲，遠佞人。鄭聲淫，佞人殆。」

知斯三者，則知所以修身；知所以修身，則知所以治人；知所以治人，則知所以治天下國家矣。

是集義所生者，非義襲而取之也。行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰：「告子未嘗知義，以其外之也。」

易

頤，貞吉。養正則吉也。觀頤，觀其所養也；自求口實，觀其自養也。

君子以正位凝命。

六爻之動，三極之道也。是故君子所居而安者，易之序也；所樂而玩者，爻之辭也。

復以自知，恒以一德。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Yan Yuan asked about governing a state. The Master said: “Follow the calendar of Xia, ride in the carriage of Yin, and wear the ceremonial cap of Zhou. For music, use the Shao dance. Banish the music of Zheng and keep glib talkers at a distance. The music of Zheng is licentious, and glib talkers are dangerous.”

Knowing these three things, one knows how to cultivate oneself; knowing how to cultivate oneself, one knows how to govern others; knowing how to govern others, one knows how to govern all under Heaven, the states, and the families.

It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds; it cannot be acquired through an isolated act of righteousness. If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, it starves. Thus I said: “Gaozi has never understood righteousness, for he regards it as external.”

Book of Changes

“Nourishment: steadfast correctness brings good fortune.” Nourishing what is correct brings good fortune. “Observe nourishment”: observe what one nourishes. “Seek sustenance for one’s own mouth”: observe how one nourishes oneself.

The noble man thereby rectifies his position and consolidates his mandate.

The movements of the six lines embody the Way of the Three Ultimates—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. Thus, what the noble man rests in and finds peace in is the ordering of the Changes; what he delights in and ponders is the wording attached to the lines.

Through Return, one knows oneself; through Constancy, one makes one’s virtue steadfast.

text:
書
詢于四岳闢四門明四目達四聰
任官惟賢才左右惟其人臣爲上爲德爲
下爲民其難其慎惟和惟一
志以道寧言以道接
相我受民和我庶獄庶慎時則勿有間之
自一話一言我則末惟成德之彥以乂
我受民
詩
===
蠶月條桑取彼斧斨以伐遠揚猗彼女桑
七月鳴鵙八月載績
戎車既安如輊如軒四牡既佶既佶且閑
薄伐獫狁至于大原文武吉甫萬邦爲
憲
訏謨定命遠猶辰告
龍旂承祀六轡耳耳春秋匪解享祀不忒
皇皇后帝皇祖后稷享以騂犧是饗是
宜降福既多周公皇祖亦其福女

書

詢于四岳，闢四門，明四目，達四聰。

任官惟賢才，左右惟其人。臣爲上爲德，爲下爲民。其難其慎，惟和惟一。

志以道寧，言以道接。

相我受民，和我庶獄庶慎，時則勿有間之。自一話一言，我則末惟成德之彥，以乂我受民。

詩

蠶月條桑，取彼斧斨，以伐遠揚，猗彼女桑。七月鳴鵙，八月載績。

戎車既安，如輊如軒。四牡既佶，既佶且閑。薄伐獫狁，至于大原。文武吉甫，萬邦爲憲。

訏謨定命，遠猶辰告。

龍旂承祀，六轡耳耳。春秋匪解，享祀不忒。皇皇后帝，皇祖后稷，享以騂犧，是饗是宜。降福既多，周公皇祖，亦其福女。
translation_en:
Book of Documents (Shu)

He consulted the Four Mountains, opened the four gates, made clear his vision in all four directions, and ensured that reports from all four directions reached his ears.

Appoint only the worthy and talented to office; place only suitable men at your side. Ministers serve their sovereign above by cultivating his virtue, and those below by serving the people. Treat this task as difficult and exercise caution; be harmonious and single-minded.

Let your purposes be settled through the Way, and let your words accord with the Way.

Assist me with the people entrusted to me; bring harmony to all my judicial proceedings and all affairs requiring care, and allow no interruption in this. In every utterance and every word, I shall ultimately look to men of perfected virtue [?] to govern the people entrusted to me.

Book of Odes (Shi)

In the silkworm month they prune the mulberries. Taking axes and hatchets, they cut the high-reaching branches and bend down the young mulberry shoots. In the seventh month the shrike calls; in the eighth month they begin spinning.

The war chariots are steady, now dipping forward, now rising. The four stallions are sturdy, sturdy and well trained. They march against the Xianyun, reaching Dayuan. Jifu, accomplished in civil and military affairs, is a model for the myriad states.

Great counsels establish commands; far-reaching plans are announced at the proper time.

Dragon banners attend the sacrifices; the six reins hang gently. In spring and autumn they are never remiss, and their sacrificial offerings never depart from the proper forms. To the august Lord on High and the august ancestor Hou Ji they offer a reddish-brown sacrificial ox. The offering is accepted and deemed fitting, and abundant blessings descend. The Duke of Zhou and the august ancestors will likewise bless you.

text:

春齊人陳人曹人伐宋〔莊公十有四年〕冬
公會晋侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾子滕
子薛伯杞伯小邾子齊世子光伐鄭十
有二月已亥同盟于戲〔襄公九年〕
荆人來聘〔莊公二十有三年〕
夏齊人伐我北鄙〔僖公二十有六年〕春王
二月秦人入滑〔僖公三十有三年〕
冬十有二月戊午晋人秦人戰于河曲〔文〕
===

禮記
博聞强識而讓敦善行而不怠謂之君子
樂也者聖人之所樂也而可以善民心其
感人深其移風易俗故先王著其教焉
是故君子議道自己而置法以民
程功積事推賢而進達之

春秋

translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

In spring, men of Qi, Chen, and Cao attacked Song. 〔Fourteenth year of Duke Zhuang〕 In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Lesser Zhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the jihai day [?], they concluded a joint covenant at Xi. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xiang〕

Men of Jing came on a diplomatic visit. 〔Twenty-third year of Duke Zhuang〕

In summer, men of Qi attacked our northern borderlands. 〔Twenty-sixth year of Duke Xi〕 In spring, in the second month of the royal calendar, men of Qin entered Hua. 〔Thirty-third year of Duke Xi〕

In winter, in the twelfth month, on the wuwu day, men of Jin and Qin fought at Hequ. 〔Twelfth year of Duke Wen〕

Book of Rites (Liji)

One who is widely learned and has a strong memory, yet remains modest, and who earnestly practices good conduct without flagging, is called a gentleman.

Music is what the sages delight in, and it can make the people's hearts good. It moves people deeply and transforms their manners and customs; therefore the former kings established instruction in it.

Thus the gentleman, in deliberating on the Way, begins with himself, and in establishing laws takes the people as his basis.

Assess accomplishments and reckon accumulated service; recommend the worthy and advance them to office.

translation_en:
…enlightened rulers: were there among them any who came close to the learning of the mind practiced by the ancient sage emperors and kings? We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new order and established the supreme standard. At the beginning of his reign, he first composed the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun); he also ordered Grand Secretary Wu Chen and others to compile material concerning three matters into the Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu). When our Emperor Chengzu Wen succeeded to the imperial line and inherited its foundations, he compiled the Essential Methods of Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa) and personally wrote its preface. In the time of our Emperor Xianzong Chun, he gathered the most authoritative discussions from ancient and recent times and produced the Great Instructions of the Hall of Literary Brilliance (Wenhua daxun).

These four books now stand as instruction for posterity, shining as brightly as the sun and stars. Can you explain in detail the guiding principles and essentials of each? Moreover, do their underlying purposes indeed accord with the learning of the mind practiced by the ancient sage emperors and kings? The works of the two founding emperors and Xianzong bear different titles, but are their underlying principles the same or not?

Now our sage emperor has succeeded to the throne and daily attends the Classics Colloquium. His Confucian ministers wish to assist his sagely learning. We ask whether all these books may be drawn upon for…

問：儒者云：「西漢尚經術，東漢崇節義。」史言之，漢世良吏爲盛。蓋漢去三代未遠，士習吏治猶近古也。嘗竊疑之：謂西漢尚經術，是則然矣，攷其時以節義表著者亦衆也；謂東漢崇節義，是則然矣，攷其時以經術著稱者亦衆也。今可各指其人而言之歟？或謂西漢之士借六藝以文奸，東漢之士甘危言以就戮，然則何貴其尚經術、崇節義歟？班史傳循吏，所載無非郡守，而曰令若長，何以不聞于時？范史傳循吏，所載率令若長，而郡守何以不多述歟？惟時若趙、張，若邊、延輩，
translation_en:
…to be expounded in lectures? At the beginning of the dynasty, the Classics Colloquium had no fixed venue; later it was established in the Wenhua Hall. Why was this? There are now proposals to offer counsel after the lectures have concluded. Was this also practiced during the reigns of our imperial ancestors? An ancient saying holds that those conducting the Classics Colloquium bear responsibility for whether the ruler’s virtue is perfected. We wish to hear your views. You gentlemen should respectfully set them forth.

Question: Confucian scholars say, “The Western Han esteemed classical learning; the Eastern Han honored integrity and righteousness.” Historians say that the Han excelled in worthy officials. Since the Han was not far removed from the Three Dynasties, the habits of its scholars and the administration of its officials still resembled those of antiquity. Yet I have privately had doubts about this. To say that the Western Han esteemed classical learning is indeed correct; but examination of that period shows that many also distinguished themselves through integrity and righteousness. To say that the Eastern Han honored integrity and righteousness is indeed correct; but examination of that period shows that many were also renowned for classical learning. Can you now identify the individuals in each category and discuss them? Some say that Western Han scholars borrowed the Six Classics to cloak their wickedness, while Eastern Han scholars willingly spoke uncompromisingly and thereby met execution. If so, what was praiseworthy about their esteem for classical learning and their honoring of integrity and righteousness? In the biographies of exemplary officials in Ban’s History of the Han, all those recorded are commandery administrators. Why, then, do we hear of no county magistrates or county chiefs of that time? In the biographies of exemplary officials in Fan’s History of the Later Han, those recorded are mostly county magistrates or county chiefs. Why are so few commandery administrators discussed? Now, men of those times such as Zhao and Zhang, or Bian and Yan…

text:
俱赫然稱能矣何以不列之循吏歟夫
士人言治必曰三代廼今天下士習日
漓吏治日急不逮漢遠甚憂世者能無
太息乎不識何修而可以返之古也諸
士彊學待問有年矣必有泂於衷者幸

問記稱儒有博學而不窮篤行而不倦而

者無幾也及考遺書所載有謂循其言
可以入道者則管仲荀卿杜預三子耳
又有謂近似儒者氣象則董仲舒毛萇
揚雄三人耳夫循之可以入道必有道
之言也今觀經區之敷言新書之作訓
與夫經傳之集註其學信辯博矣果可

translation_en:
…all were conspicuously acclaimed for their ability. Why, then, were they not included among the Exemplary Officials? When scholars discuss government, they invariably invoke the Three Dynasties. Yet today, throughout the realm, scholars’ standards grow daily more debased, and official administration daily more oppressive, falling far short even of the Han. Can those concerned for the world refrain from deep sighs? What should be cultivated to restore the ways of antiquity? You scholars have devoted yourselves to learning and awaited such questions for years. Surely you have insights deep within your hearts [?]; kindly explain them clearly to me.

Question: The Record of Rites states, “Among the Confucian scholars are those who learn broadly without exhausting their studies and act earnestly without tiring.” Yet Master Cheng says, “The gentleman as a Confucian scholar learns for his own sake.” If one truly learns for one’s own sake, learning is not merely a matter of breadth, nor conduct merely a matter of exertion. Otherwise, would this not approach becoming engrossed in external things and vaunting one’s reputation? Judging the Confucian scholars of the age by this standard, few meet Master Cheng’s expectations. Yet when we examine the surviving sayings recorded in his Collected Writings (Yishu), those whose words, he says, can lead one into the Way are just Guan Zhong, Xun Qing, and Du Yu. Again, those whom he describes as approaching the bearing of a Confucian scholar are just Dong Zhongshu, Mao Chang, and Yang Xiong. If following their words can lead one into the Way, those words must embody the Way. Now, examining the expositions in Jingqu [?], the teachings set forth in the New Writings (Xinshu), and the collected annotations on the Classic and its Commentary, their learning is certainly discriminating and extensive. But can they truly be said to possess the Way? Or did he find a single saying worth adopting and disregard everything else? And what exactly did he find worth adopting? Lowering the curtain to study in seclusion and applying oneself with profound concentration may well be called…

translation_en:
…steadfast conduct; yet those who demand perfection still have criticisms to make. By associating with Dong Xian and Wang Mang, Yang Xiong had already compromised his integrity in matters of great principle. Although Mao Chang’s commentary on the Odes survives, scarcely any of his other words or deeds appear in the records. On what evidence, then, are these men all described as close to being Confucians? Xun Qing elucidated kingship and hegemony, expounded rites and music, and took upon himself the Way of Zhongni and Zigong; yet he is ranked alongside Guan Zhong and Du Yu. Among the Confucians of the two Han dynasties, many were conspicuous for their classical learning and virtuous conduct. Why could they not be ranked with those three? Master Cheng, as an eminent Confucian [?], would surely have been cautious in granting approval. These words of his were not merely an assessment of the six men: they presumably showed students the essentials of broadening their knowledge and cultivating virtue, and of examining antiquity while living in the present. If you can explain how the Way may be entered through their words and in what respects they approached the Confucian ideal, you will have thought through more than half of what learning requires.
Question: Managing the affairs of the realm is difficult; managing situations of danger, uncertainty, and wavering allegiance is harder still. Reading history, I have come upon several incidents which, when I closed the book and reflected upon them, made me recognize that the ancients had achievements beyond our reach. Early in the Han dynasty, the feudal princes were powerful, and the situation was dangerous. Someone then proposed dividing their kingdoms, and before long the princes were weakened. Did this strategy also have a precedent on which it rested? At the end of the Tang dynasty, the military governors arrogated power to themselves, and the situation was urgent. Someone then proposed a plan to take control of their troops, and the military governorships were consequently eliminated. How was this plan devised? 請遣使就勞，因頒獻錢，致正巳大慙者，誰歟？西夏納款，因言國饑，乞粟百萬，蓋覘宋也。時有請具糧京師，詔彼自取，致謂朝廷有人者，誰歟？野利，元昊之貴臣也。議稱太尉，發言盈庭矣。或者爭以片言而遽止，言何卒中歟？趙密，張俊之部將也。拒命不分，挾權相疑矣。或者抽以入衛而無辭，慮何卒辦歟？夫臨大事，決大議，不動聲色而措天下於泰山之安者，社稷之臣也。古人有焉。今論其世，尚相與繹言之，主司將以觀他日所大受者。

translation_en:
…who was it who proposed sending an envoy to convey appreciation to him and then distributing the money he had offered, thereby putting Li Zhengyi [正巳 in the transcription, apparently for 正已] deeply to shame? Western Xia tendered its submission, then claimed that its country was suffering famine and requested a million measures of grain; its purpose was to probe the Song. Who was it who proposed assembling the grain at the capital and issuing an edict that they should come to collect it themselves, prompting them to say that the court had capable men? Yeli was a high-ranking minister of Yuanhao. When conferring on him the title of Defender-in-Chief was discussed, the court was full of voices. Someone opposed it with a brief statement, and the proposal was immediately halted. How did his words prove so apt? Zhao Mi was a subordinate commander of Zhang Jun. He defied orders and would not divide [his troops?]; wielding military power, they regarded one another with suspicion. Someone transferred him to service in the imperial guard, leaving him no grounds to object. How did this plan succeed? Those who confront great affairs and decide momentous questions without betraying agitation in voice or expression, and settle the realm as securely as Mount Tai, are ministers who safeguard the state. Such men existed in antiquity. Now, in discussing their times, let us examine and expound these matters together. The chief examiners will thereby judge your capacity to undertake great responsibilities in the future.

In its exactions from the people, it does not exhaust their strength; in regulating expenditure, it does not exhaust its resources. translation_en: …grow greater by the day. Even if we wish to keep expenditure within revenue, there are circumstances in which we cannot, and the fiscal authorities report that the treasury is exhausted. By what means can this be remedied? Moreover, transporting treasury funds to meet frontier expenses was not practiced in the time of our imperial ancestors. During the Zhengtong reign, when emergencies arose near the frontier, measured amounts of surplus funds were disbursed to assist. Examination of that period shows that the treasuries were overflowing, and the sums disbursed were minute. Yet today the funds sent annually to the various frontiers amount to more than ten or a hundred times those sums. How, then, did this begin? The extent of the frontier has not increased, nor have troop numbers grown. In the past, when treasury reserves were not disbursed, the various frontier regions must have had means of supporting themselves. Yet now, if the annual allocation is slightly reduced or transport slightly delayed, frontier officials send urgent appeals one after another. Why is this? Those discussing the matter say that expenditure has no bounds because established fiscal arrangements are unsettled. Is this so or not? Establishing such arrangements would certainly provide a lasting plan, but how are the immediate emergencies to be met in the meantime? The regular expenditures administered by the fiscal authorities are numerous. Is frontier military provisioning really the sole drain on financial resources? In the middle periods of the Han and Song dynasties, funds likewise fell short. The Han employed the price-stabilization system, and the government had ample resources; the Song established the Office for the Formulation of Regulations, yet both state and people were impoverished. text:
第壹塲
四書
顏淵問爲邦子曰行夏之時乘殷之輅服
周之冕樂則韶舞放鄭聲遠佞人鄭聲
淫佞人殆
胡載道
同考試官教諭沈批孔子告顏淵天德王道
之蘊盡於此章發之是作精醇典雅又善發孔顏之蘊
矣宜錄以式
===
同考試官知州宋批簡明雅潤無一浮語發
揮王道悉矣非其善于爲邦者與宜錄以式
同考試官推官王批矩度嚴整詞理精醇孔
子告顏子爲邦之道發揮明盡宜錄以式多士
考試官右中允張批辭不費而理足取之
考試官右諭德丁批純雅
大賢問治聖人示以治道而申其防焉蓋經邦
有道也舉其道而尤慎其防焉治其庶幾乎昔
顏淵有爲邦之問蓋將以得諸德行者而發之

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

顏淵問爲邦。子曰：「行夏之時，乘殷之輅，服周之冕，樂則韶舞。放鄭聲，遠佞人。鄭聲淫，佞人殆。」

胡載道

同考試官教諭沈批：「孔子告顏淵，天德王道之蘊盡於此章。發之是作，精醇典雅，又善發孔顏之蘊矣。宜錄以式。」

同考試官知州宋批：「簡明雅潤，無一浮語，發揮王道悉矣。非其善于爲邦者與？宜錄以式。」

同考試官推官王批：「矩度嚴整，詞理精醇，孔子告顏子爲邦之道，發揮明盡。宜錄以式多士。」

考試官右中允張批：「辭不費而理足，取之。」

考試官右諭德丁批：「純雅。」

大賢問治，聖人示以治道而申其防焉。蓋經邦有道也，舉其道而尤慎其防焉，治其庶幾乎！昔顏淵有爲邦之問，蓋將以得諸德行者而發之
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Yan Yuan asked about governing a state. The Master said: “Follow the calendar of Xia, ride in the carriage of Yin, and wear the ceremonial cap of Zhou. For music, use the Shao dance. Banish the music of Zheng and keep glib talkers at a distance. The music of Zheng is licentious; glib talkers are dangerous.”

Hu Zaidao

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor: “In Confucius’s instruction to Yan Yuan, the full significance of heavenly virtue and the kingly Way is contained in this chapter. This composition expounds it with refinement, purity, classical dignity, and elegance; it also brings out well the deeper meaning of Confucius and Yan Yuan. It should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Song, Department Magistrate: “Concise, clear, elegant, and polished, without a single empty phrase, it fully expounds the kingly Way. Is its author not someone skilled in governing a state? It should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Prefectural Judge: “Its structure is rigorous and orderly, its language and reasoning refined and pure. It expounds clearly and fully the way of governing a state that Confucius taught Master Yan. It should be recorded as a model for the many scholars.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Rectifier: “The language is economical, yet the reasoning is complete. Accept it.”

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: “Pure and elegant.”

A great worthy asked about government; the sage showed him the way to govern and further emphasized the precautions it required. For there is a proper way to order a state. If one follows that way and takes particular care over its safeguards, good government may surely be within reach! In former times, Yan Yuan asked about governing a state, intending to give expression to what he had attained in virtuous conduct …

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事業也孔子因告之曰政有因革道貴變通爲
邦者審此而已彼時以作事吾嘗仰稽三正而
得夏時焉語時正而令善者莫尚乎此也時之
行也其惟夏乎輅以昭德吾嘗上考王制而得
殷輅焉語崇朴而辨等者莫尚乎此也輅之乘
也其惟殷乎冕以稱章服華不靡而費不奢者
惟周冕則然矣易服色者舍是將奚服哉樂以
和神人既盡美而又盡善者惟韶舞則然矣同
律呂者舍是將奚法哉行此四者而百王不能
===
易矣至若邦有鄭聲又人所易溺也必禁而放
之凡宗廟朝廷勿使作於其上焉邦有佞人又
人所易惑也必屏而遠之凡股肱耳目勿使雜
於其間焉是何也鄭聲流辟邪散蕩性情而亂
雅樂淫莫有甚焉者也佞人卑諂辯給肆利口
而覆邦家殆莫有甚焉者也斯二者又可以一
日不謹哉吁慎斯術也而治道其易易矣回也
如有用之執此以往可也抑因是而知聖人之
蘊因顏子以發也四代禮樂以語爲邦克己復

punctuated: 事業也。孔子因告之曰：「政有因革，道貴變通，爲邦者審此而已。彼時以作事，吾嘗仰稽三正而得夏時焉。語時正而令善者，莫尚乎此也。時之行也，其惟夏乎！輅以昭德，吾嘗上考王制而得殷輅焉。語崇朴而辨等者，莫尚乎此也。輅之乘也，其惟殷乎！冕以稱章服，華不靡而費不奢者，惟周冕則然矣。易服色者，舍是將奚服哉？樂以和神人，既盡美而又盡善者，惟韶舞則然矣。同律呂者，舍是將奚法哉？行此四者，而百王不能易矣。至若邦有鄭聲，又人所易溺也，必禁而放之，凡宗廟朝廷勿使作於其上焉。邦有佞人，又人所易惑也，必屏而遠之，凡股肱耳目勿使雜於其間焉。是何也？鄭聲流辟邪散，蕩性情而亂雅樂，淫莫有甚焉者也。佞人卑諂辯給，肆利口而覆邦家，殆莫有甚焉者也。斯二者，又可以一日不謹哉？吁！慎斯術也，而治道其易易矣。回也，如有用之，執此以往可也。」抑因是而知聖人之蘊，因顏子以發也。四代禮樂以語爲邦，克己復
translation_en:
…in practical achievements. Confucius therefore told him: “Government involves both retaining and changing established practices; the Way values adaptation to changing circumstances. Those who govern a state need only discern this. As for the calendar used to undertake affairs, I have examined the three systems for fixing the beginning of the year and selected the Xia calendar. For correctness in marking the seasons and excellence in seasonal ordinances, nothing surpasses it. In adopting a calendar, should we not choose that of Xia? Carriages serve to manifest virtue. I have examined the institutions of former kings and selected the Yin carriage. For honoring simplicity while distinguishing ranks, nothing surpasses it. In choosing a carriage to ride in, should we not choose that of Yin? The ceremonial cap should accord with the patterned robes. For elegance without extravagance and expenditure without excess, only the Zhou cap meets the requirement. When changing the colors of ceremonial dress, what could one wear if one abandoned this? Music harmonizes spirits and human beings. For perfection both in beauty and in goodness, only the Shao dance meets the requirement. In harmonizing the pitch standards, what could one take as a model if one abandoned this? Put these four things into practice, and a hundred successive kings could not alter them.

“As for the music of Zheng within the state, people are easily enthralled by it. It must be prohibited and banished; never allow it to be performed in the ancestral temples or at court. As for glib flatterers within the state, people are easily deluded by them. They must be excluded and kept at a distance; never allow them to mingle among the ministers who serve as the ruler’s limbs, ears, and eyes. Why is this? The music of Zheng is wayward, depraved, and unrestrained: it unsettles human dispositions and feelings and disrupts proper ceremonial music. Nothing exceeds it in licentiousness. Glib flatterers are servile and fawning, clever in argument and ready in speech: they give free rein to their sharp tongues and overturn states and ruling houses. Nothing exceeds them in danger. Can one neglect vigilance against these two things for even a single day? Ah! Attend carefully to these methods, and the way of governing will become very easy indeed. Hui, if anyone should employ you, you may hold fast to these principles and proceed.”

“From this, moreover, we recognize that the sage’s deepest teachings were brought forth through Master Yan. The rites and music of the four dynasties were discussed in speaking of governing a state; overcoming the self and returning to…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以力行近也勇以知耻近也察識於求端用六
之始而向往之不迷則必於學而知好也於行
而知力也於耻而知奮也體驗於反躬自治之
餘而進爲之不悖内以克全所性而達德可立
外以允迪厥猷而達道可行身之修也亦惟修
此三者故全耳而不裕於治乎吾知以己觀人
彼我異而理一也知所以修身則見其治人者
無以異於治夫己凡出身加民達鼓舞作興之
用所以知之明處之當者於己取之而已矣道
===
豈遠乎哉以一人觀萬人眾寡殊而人一也知
所以治人則見其治天下國家之眾者無以異
於治夫寡凡舉此加彼極裁成輔相之宜所以
遠有望近不厭者善推所爲而已矣術豈多乎
哉夫以身之修也達於天下國家之治此入德
行道之功不可缺也天下國家之治也而本於
身修此取人行政之基貴先豫也君欲圖政盍
亦求諸己矣嘗考皐陶矢慎修之謨傅說納乃
來之誨帝王治本於身尚矣哀公奚足語此而

punctuated: 以力行近也，勇以知耻近也。察識於求端用六之始，而向往之不迷，則必於學而知好也，於行而知力也，於耻而知奮也。體驗於反躬自治之餘，而進爲之不悖，内以克全所性而達德可立，外以允迪厥猷而達道可行。身之修也，亦惟修此三者故全耳，而不裕於治乎？吾知以己觀人，彼我異而理一也。知所以修身，則見其治人者無以異於治夫己。凡出身加民，達鼓舞作興之用，所以知之明、處之當者，於己取之而已矣，道豈遠乎哉？以一人觀萬人，眾寡殊而人一也。知所以治人，則見其治天下國家之眾者無以異於治夫寡。凡舉此加彼，極裁成輔相之宜，所以遠有望、近不厭者，善推所爲而已矣，術豈多乎哉？夫以身之修也，達於天下國家之治，此入德行道之功不可缺也。天下國家之治也，而本於身修，此取人行政之基貴先豫也。君欲圖政，盍亦求諸己矣？嘗考皐陶矢慎修之謨，傅說納乃來之誨，帝王治本於身尚矣。哀公奚足語此，而

…is approached through strenuous practice, and courage is approached through knowing shame. If one exercises discernment at the outset of seeking a starting point and applying effort [?], without losing sight of one’s direction, then in learning one will know to delight in it, in practice one will know to exert oneself, and in feeling shame one will know to rouse oneself. Through personal experience gained from self-examination and self-discipline, one advances in practice without going astray. Inwardly, one fully realizes one’s endowed nature, so that the universally applicable virtues can be established; outwardly, one faithfully follows the proper course, so that the universally applicable Way can be practiced. Cultivating oneself becomes complete simply through cultivating these three. Would this not also provide ample resources for governing?

I know that, when one considers others through oneself, others and oneself differ, but the principle is one. Knowing how to cultivate oneself, one sees that governing others is no different from governing oneself. Whenever one extends what is in oneself to the people and fully exercises the power to inspire and invigorate them, clear understanding and appropriate handling of affairs are drawn from oneself alone. How could the Way be distant? When one considers ten thousand people through a single person, the many and the few differ, but their humanity is one. Knowing how to govern people, one sees that governing the multitudes of the world, the state, and the family is no different from governing the few. Whenever one extends what is done here to what lies beyond, fully realizing the appropriate work of shaping and assisting, those far away look to one with hope and those nearby do not tire of one simply because one skillfully extends what one already does. How could this require many techniques?

To extend self-cultivation to the governance of the world, the state, and the family requires indispensable work in entering into virtue and practicing the Way. That governance of the world, the state, and the family rests upon self-cultivation means that this foundation for selecting men and administering government must be prepared beforehand. If a ruler wishes to undertake government, why should he not seek its basis within himself? I have examined how Gao Yao set forth his counsel on careful self-cultivation and how Fu Yue presented his admonition that ‘they will come to you.’ The principle that emperors and kings base their government upon themselves is ancient indeed. How was Duke Ai worthy of being spoken to about this? Yet…

…then the vital energy (qi) is full; hence nurturing it must depend on righteousness. How could those who regard righteousness as external understand this? When properly nurtured, this energy indeed fills Heaven and Earth and accords with the Way and righteousness. But at the outset of nurturing it, what work must one undertake? By examining the subtlest stirrings of thought and desiring nothing that one ought not to desire, one discriminates righteousness with the utmost precision. By holding fast to it in manifest responses to things and doing nothing that one ought not to do, one develops righteousness to its fullest extent. From accordance with righteousness at a single moment, one extends it until there is no moment without righteousness. Thus, free of shame and embarrassment, one possesses within the heart the full form of this vast, flowing energy. Could one say that briefly following righteousness, without any depth of attainment, enables one suddenly to seize its substance? From accordance with righteousness in a single affair, one extends it until no affair is without righteousness. Thus, free of anxiety and fear, one possesses within oneself the complete efficacy of this vast, flowing energy. Could one say that an affair’s chance conformity with righteousness, without gradual accumulation, enables one fortuitously to attain its efficacy?

If a single affair is righteous, but one’s other conduct is not necessarily all righteous, inward examination will surely reveal grounds for remorse, and doubt and fear will follow. Can righteousness, then, be seized through an isolated act? Even if many affairs are righteous, so long as a single action remains at odds with it, self-examination will still find one wanting in rectitude, and regret and shame will not be banished. Can righteousness, then, fail to be accumulated? When righteousness is accumulated, the heart is satisfied and the vital energy does not starve. This energy is the aid of the will. It is internal, and therefore can be generated but cannot be seized. Righteousness is the heart’s rule. Righteousness, too, is internal, and therefore can be accumulated but cannot be acquired through an isolated act.

When I say that Gaozi never understood righteousness, it is precisely because he treated it as external. To treat righteousness as external is already to force one’s understanding into an artificial form and thereby lose, from the outset, the source of nurturing the energy through rectitude. However laborious one’s efforts at forcible restraint, one will not…

…withstand the harm caused by his contrived efforts. His unmoved mind is merely something seized through an isolated act of righteousness: can his vital force ultimately avoid depletion? This is what distinguishes me from Gaozi. Moreover, a discussion of human nature that does not discuss vital force is incomplete. Mencius declared that human nature is good, yet also advanced this teaching on nourishing vital force. Principle depends on vital force to take form; its vast, flowing character is precisely what is meant by goodness. Blinded by the mistaken belief that righteousness is external, Gaozi offered the analogies of willow wood and swirling water, going so far as to identify vital force deprived of proper nourishment with human nature. Fearing harm to the human mind, Mencius carefully refuted him. Was he speaking solely for Gongsun Chou?

Book of Changes
“The noble man rectifies his position and consolidates the Mandate.”
By Zhuang Yunzhong.

Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “The noble man presides over the cauldron and makes virtue the foundation for praying to Heaven that the Mandate may endure. This composition develops the meaning clearly and fully; it is a refined exposition of the meaning of the Changes.”

Associate Examiner Chen, metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “It develops the purport of the noble man’s rectifying his position and consolidating the Mandate without empty rhetoric. Precise, pertinent, earnest, and thorough, it surely comes from someone deeply versed in the study of the Changes. It should be recorded as a model.”

Examiner Zhang, Right Mentor, comments: “Refined and lucid; worthy of selection.”

Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher, comments: “Developing this topic in a single continuous line of argument is indeed appropriate.”

The noble man maintains rectitude in order to receive Heaven’s blessings. The august Mandate is not easy to preserve; the noble man consolidates it by rectifying his position. How well he embodies the Changes! Now, the ruler’s position is bestowed by Heaven. By contemplating the image of the Cauldron hexagram, the noble man apprehends the way to consolidate the Mandate.

text:
以鼎之能凝其所受之實者惟其正也君之能
凝其所受之命者亦惟其正也於焉思天命之
難諶也而建皇極以宅尊期不失乎上帝寵綏
之重念大命之靡常也而順帝則以出治欲克
膺夫維皇曆數之傳不動而敬矣雖視聽言動
亦必以禮焉惟精惟一以執厥中務俾自天降
之者自我享之也不顯亦臨矣雖出入起居罔
有不欽焉無為無思以守至正務俾自天申之
者自我承之也是何也表正之體孰斯履位之
===

也否則敗厥度者忝厥位而豈祈天之道也哉
元良之道懋斯帝德之罔愆而福履之錫於身
者始可以保之於無疆也否則縱逸豫者滅厥

敗者一而已矣𠤎易之功斯其至與抑鼎重噐
也主之誠難矣古之明王所以修厥身允德協
于下者凡以奠此一鼎也後之人君不務修身以

…For the cauldron can secure the contents it receives only because it stands upright; the ruler can likewise secure the mandate he receives only through his uprightness. Thus he considers how difficult it is to rely upon Heaven’s mandate and establishes the sovereign standard in occupying his exalted position, hoping not to forfeit the weighty favor and protection of the Lord on High. He reflects that the great mandate is not constant and follows the Lord’s rules in administering government, seeking to prove worthy of receiving the transmitted succession of sovereign rule. Even without acting, he is reverent; in looking, listening, speaking, and moving, he invariably accords with ritual propriety. Through refinement and singleness of purpose, he holds fast to the mean, striving to ensure that what Heaven bestows he himself may enjoy. Even where nothing is manifest, he conducts himself as though under scrutiny; in going out and coming in, rising and resting, he is never without reverence. Without contrived action or thought, he maintains perfect uprightness, striving to ensure that what Heaven renews he himself may receive.

Why is this? Only when his embodiment of exemplary uprightness has matured [?], and he occupies his position without fault, can the bright mandate that has descended upon his person be extended without lapse. Otherwise, one who ruins the standards of his conduct disgraces his position: how could this be the way to seek Heaven’s favor? Only when the way of supreme goodness flourishes, and sovereign virtue is without error, can the blessings bestowed upon him be preserved without limit. Otherwise, one who indulges in ease and pleasure destroys his virtue: how could this be the foundation for perpetuating the mandate? His making his position upright is thus precisely like setting the cauldron securely in place. His securing the mandate is precisely like the cauldron’s receiving its contents without spoiling them. Does not the efficacy of transformation through the Changes [?] reach its utmost here?

Yet the cauldron is a weighty vessel, and truly difficult to preside over. “Through Return, one knows oneself; through Constancy, one makes one’s virtue constant.”
By Wang Zhao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The topic is intrinsically subtle and intricate, and difficult to express. This composition probes its most profound subtleties. Its exposition of knowing oneself and making one’s virtue constant is lucid, precise, and apt. Here is someone deeply versed in the Book of Changes.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Topics concerning principle are the hardest to expound. This essay, however, displays outstanding insight, with language that is precise and penetrating. Reading it, one finds it quite dazzling. It is fitting to record it as a model for the many scholars.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: Its explanation of principle is clear and distinct.

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent: A precise and subtle composition.

The Great Commentary sets forth the functions of Return and Constancy, encompassing the work of refined discernment and single-mindedness. To scrutinize with precision and hold fast with single-mindedness is the consummate achievement of cultivating virtue. The functions of Return and Constancy encompass this. Is not the Book of Changes the standard for learning to become a sage? The Great Commentary discusses nine hexagrams; at this point it seems to say: in the gentleman’s learning, what benefits outward affairs is indeed valued for excellence in practice, but what provides inward preparation is especially valued for depth of apprehension. Principle must be illuminated within the mind before there can be true insight. When truth and delusion become intermingled, understanding is obscured. Now Return is slight, yet distinguishes among things. When remorse and awakening reach their fullest extent, the mind’s original, open and numinous substance is preserved whole; the subtle incipiencies of the precarious human mind and the subtle mind of the Way are perhaps apprehended in solitary awareness, discernment, and recognition…

□而真切之良心以著天人之介殆不昧於反
觀私所本無也吾自克之則幾希之良適得其
體者炯然吾自知之人莫能測也理所固有也
吾自還之則發見之端不失其常者灼然吾自
知之無待於外也是蓋內無所蔽知通於性矣
其真見有如此者善必有諸已而後有定力也
久暫殊致德斯岐矣迺兹恒雜而不厭焉則道
心為主不以時之先後而有異同天理常存不
以遇之順逆而為操舍行道有得守為終身之

相與眩驚之而不貳以二不參以三也是蓋外

…[illegible; ?], and the genuine, earnest moral heart becomes manifest; through inward reflection, the boundary between Heaven and human desires is surely no longer obscured. Selfishness is originally absent from us. When I myself overcome it, the slight measure of goodness that distinguishes humanity shines clearly in its proper substance. I know this myself; others cannot fathom it. Principle is inherently ours. When I myself restore it, the first signs of its manifestation shine distinctly, without departing from their constant norm. I know this myself, without depending upon anything external. Thus nothing obscures the inner self, and knowledge penetrates our nature. Such is genuine insight.
Goodness must be present within oneself before one can possess steadfast resolve. If enduring and momentary effort lead in different directions, virtue becomes divided. Yet here Constancy means encountering complexity without becoming wearied. The mind of the Way then governs, admitting no difference between earlier and later times; Heaven’s principle remains continually present, neither retained nor abandoned according to whether circumstances are favorable or adverse. Having attained something through practicing the Way, one holds to it as a lifelong foundation. Though encounters with things and external stimuli together assail and seek to capture it, they leave no trace in hearing and sight and do not impinge upon the workings of the mind. Making goodness the master and bringing everything into unity, one establishes an unchanging rule. Though deviant doctrines and perverse conduct together bewilder and alarm one, one is not divided in two by two things, nor in three by three. Thus nothing external displaces one, and virtue rests where it should abide. Such is steadfast resolve.
When principle is just returning, scrutinizing it with precision is the beginning of knowing; once principle has been attained, holding to it with singleness is the culmination of practice. The complete achievement of the sages’ learning is thus present. What difficulty, then, can anxiety and adversity pose? Moreover, the injunction to be precise and single-minded was the method of cultivating the mind transmitted at the court of Shun. Among Confucius’s disciples, only Master Yan could be spoken of in these terms. Thus Confucius said, “He has perhaps nearly attained it!” This refers to Return. He also said, “For three months he did not depart from benevolence.” This refers to Constancy. The learning of precision and singleness was embodied in him. “In appointing officials, choose only the worthy and talented; for those at your side, choose only suitable men. Ministers serve those above through virtue and those below through service to the people. Treat this as difficult and exercise caution; seek harmony and unity.”

Gao Wenbing

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Instructor: “Appointing men to sustain unity of virtue was the deeply loyal and earnest concern of Yi Yin. This essay is dignified and classically elegant, fully bringing out the passage’s underlying meaning. It should be included as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Shao, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “Those who write on this topic frequently fail to achieve coherence and lucid exposition, which is decidedly tiresome. This composition is concise in wording yet complete in meaning, clear and refined—beyond the reach of ordinary work.”

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Adviser: “Luminous and lucid.”

A great minister, guiding his ruler, places emphasis on employing men and accordingly sets forth the proper way to appoint officials. For ministerial duties carry weighty responsibilities toward ruler and people: can one who appoints officials fail to exercise the utmost care?

It was with this that Yi Yin instructed Tai Jia. His meaning was this: as the king newly assumed his charge, unity of virtue was essential, and employing men was urgent. Could he fail to be cautious? Those charged with administering affairs are the various officials. To extend such appointments to personal favorites would be wrong. Only men of worth and talent should be assessed and then appointed; otherwise, it would be better to leave their posts vacant. Those entrusted with assisting and supporting the ruler are the men at his side…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也及匪人焉非矣必備道全美者然後任而相
之否則寧不必備也所以然者何哉蓋庶官左
右莫非臣也語其上則君為大焉而各隨其分
以佐辟君德所賴以修明者此也語其下則民
為重焉而各率其職以宅師民生所賴以潤澤
者此也所繫至矣而可以不謹耶故擇之不精
非謹也而擬議於遴選之時者必其難焉其慎
焉進之如不得已而察之尤致其詳所以度諸
始者無不至也任之不專非謹也而推誠於委
===
用之際者必惟和焉惟一焉以道則相濟而以
心則相孚所以厚其終者無弗周也夫然則庶
官皆賢左右得人而上下有攸賴矣吁王欲新
厥德也可不用情於此哉抑伊尹告歸陳德而
即繼之以論官何耶蓋人情鮮克有終使國無
其人誰與道迪哉故古之大臣既委曲以濟君
又慮其無以自代使吾身雖去而允德之克終
者如故此固尹之志也然協一之訓太甲得與
聞焉君子謂伊尹成始終之大忠信哉

者如故此固尹之志也然協一之訓太甲得與

punctuated: 也，及匪人焉，非矣。必備道全美者，然後任而相之，否則寧不必備也。所以然者何哉？蓋庶官左右，莫非臣也。語其上，則君為大焉，而各隨其分以佐辟，君德所賴以修明者此也；語其下，則民為重焉，而各率其職以宅師，民生所賴以潤澤者此也。所繫至矣，而可以不謹耶？故擇之不精，非謹也，而擬議於遴選之時者，必其難焉，其慎焉，進之如不得已，而察之尤致其詳，所以度諸始者無不至也。任之不專，非謹也，而推誠於委用之際者，必惟和焉，惟一焉，以道則相濟，而以心則相孚，所以厚其終者無弗周也。夫然，則庶官皆賢，左右得人，而上下有攸賴矣。吁！王欲新厥德也，可不用情於此哉？抑伊尹告歸，陳德而即繼之以論官，何耶？蓋人情鮮克有終，使國無其人，誰與道迪哉？故古之大臣，既委曲以濟君，又慮其無以自代，使吾身雖去，而允德之克終者如故，此固尹之志也。然協一之訓，太甲得與聞焉。君子謂伊尹成始終之大忠，信哉！
translation_en:
…are those at the ruler’s side. To extend such appointments to unworthy men would be wrong. Only those fully endowed with the Way and complete in excellence should be entrusted with office and made chief ministers; otherwise, it is better to leave the posts unfilled. Why is this so? The various officials and those at the ruler’s side are all servants of the throne. In relation to those above them, the ruler is paramount: each assists the sovereign according to his allotted responsibilities, and it is upon this that the cultivation and illumination of the ruler’s virtue depend. In relation to those below them, the people are of greatest importance: each discharges his duties to bring repose to the multitude, and it is upon this that the enrichment of the people’s livelihood depends. The stakes are of the utmost importance. How could one fail to exercise care?

Thus, to select without discrimination is not to exercise care. When deliberating over candidates, one must treat the choice as difficult and proceed cautiously, advancing a man as though only necessity compelled it and examining him with particular thoroughness. In this way, nothing is neglected in the assessment made at the outset. To employ a man without wholehearted trust is likewise not to exercise care. When sincerely entrusting him with responsibilities, there must be harmony and unity: through the Way, ruler and minister assist one another; in their hearts, they trust one another. In this way, every provision is made to ensure a sound conclusion. Then the various officials will all be worthy, the right men will stand at the ruler’s side, and both those above and those below will have someone upon whom to rely. Ah! If the king wishes to renew his virtue, can he fail to devote his heart to this?

Yet why, when Yi Yin announced his retirement, did he follow his exposition of virtue immediately with a discussion of appointments? Human beings seldom carry things through to the end. If the state lacked suitable men, who would guide the ruler along the Way? Thus the great ministers of antiquity, having assisted their rulers with painstaking care, also worried that they might have no one to succeed them. They sought to ensure that, although they themselves departed, the ruler’s ability to persevere to the end in true virtue would remain as before. This was indeed Yi Yin’s intention. Moreover, Tai Jia was able to hear his admonition concerning harmony and unity. The gentleman’s judgment that Yi Yin displayed great loyalty in bringing both the beginning and the end to completion is true indeed!

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Instructor: “The meaning is upright and pertinent; the language is rigorous and dignified. This essay expounds the essential teaching concerning the mind transmitted by the ancient sages and worthies [preceding wording doubtful: 榮古], leaving virtually nothing unexplored.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Shao, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “The other compositions generally rely on empty phrasing and ultimately elucidate nothing. This composition takes the Way as its governing principle, and its exposition of ‘finding repose’ and ‘receiving’ is especially clear and full. It reads just like the teaching concerning the mind that sages and worthies imparted to one another. A high recommendation is fully deserved.”
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Mentor: “Genuine and pertinent.”
Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: “It ably elucidates a difficult topic and may serve as a model.”
In preserving his mind and listening to words, the ruler must conform solely to the Way. If his will does not stir heedlessly but finds repose only in the Way, and if he does not heed words indiscriminately but receives them only in accordance with the Way, then inward and outward cultivation advance together. Is this not the utmost care for virtue? The intent of the Duke of Shao’s admonition to King Wu was, it would seem, to say that one who rules others must make virtue manifest and prevent wrongdoing, extending his oversight and illumination over both the Yi peoples and the Xia realm. He therefore remains vigilant and apprehensive, not daring to depart from the Way. He must guard not merely against frivolity and negligence, but especially attend to cultivation both within and without.
When the will stirs within the mind, principle and desire diverge. If one simply follows whatever arises without restraining it, the mind will wander in and out at no fixed times. The very moment a ruler forms an intention is where good fortune and misfortune, regret and disgrace originate. How could he fail to be watchful? He must therefore settle his will through the Way, expanding utter impartiality to make it the source of fitting responses. With a governing principle, the mind is receptive, never drawn astray by the ascendancy of emotions…

text:
守至正以為起知之本而無欲則静初不引於
物交凡将迎往来苟可為王心累者勿使作於
念焉則操存固而天德寧矣茲明王所以慎德
於內者乎言接於耳邪正參焉惟所聞而莫之
擇将非禮是聽也人君一納言之頃乃枉直舉
措所由關者而可不慎乎故必以道接之羣策
畢陳務求其當而不徒以遜志為賢兩端是執
務用其中而不獨以逆心為諱凡便佞捷給苟
可為王聽惑者勿使至於前焉則取舍審而聽
===
===
德聰矣茲明王所以慎德於外者乎夫以道寧
志則內欲不萌既豫受言之基以道接言則外
誘不入益為持志之助若是乎交修不容已也
而顧可役耳目貴異物耶雖然此旅人貢獒耳
未聞武王受之武王豈甘諂言有逸志者召公
道寧道接之訓不徐徐焉古大臣之忠愛類如
此世之飾言自謀務為容悅者固召公罪人也
然必間君之僻志成之則寧志又接言本也

此世之飾言自諆務爲容悅者固召公罪人也
□必聞君之僻志成之則寔志又接言本也
punctuated:
守至正以為起知之本，而無欲則静，初不引於物交。凡将迎往来，苟可為王心累者，勿使作於念焉，則操存固而天德寧矣。茲明王所以慎德於內者乎！言接於耳，邪正參焉，惟所聞而莫之擇，将非禮是聽也。人君一納言之頃，乃枉直舉措所由關者，而可不慎乎？故必以道接之，羣策畢陳，務求其當，而不徒以遜志為賢；兩端是執，務用其中，而不獨以逆心為諱。凡便佞捷給，苟可為王聽惑者，勿使至於前焉，則取舍審而聽德聰矣。茲明王所以慎德於外者乎！

夫以道寧志，則內欲不萌，既豫受言之基；以道接言，則外誘不入，益為持志之助。若是乎交修不容已也，而顧可役耳目、貴異物耶？雖然，此旅人貢獒耳，未聞武王受之。武王豈甘諂言、有逸志者？召公道寧道接之訓，不徐徐焉。古大臣之忠愛類如此。世之飾言自謀、務為容悅者，固召公罪人也。然必間君之僻志成之，則寧志又接言本也。
translation_en:
…He holds fast to perfect rectitude as the foundation for the arising of understanding [?]; free from desire, he is still, never drawn away by encounters with things. In all his responses to what comes and goes, whatever might burden the king’s mind must not be allowed to arise in his thoughts. Then his grasp and preservation of the mind will be firm, and his heavenly virtue tranquil. Is this not how an enlightened king attends carefully to virtue within? When words reach his ears, the perverse and the upright are mingled together. If he merely hears without discriminating, he will listen to what violates ritual propriety. The moment a ruler accepts someone’s words bears upon whether his appointments and measures favor the crooked or the upright: how could he fail to be cautious? He must therefore receive words according to the Way. When all proposals are presented, he must seek what is fitting, rather than deeming advice worthy merely because it accords with his wishes. He must grasp both extremes and employ the mean, rather than shunning advice merely because it runs counter to his inclinations. Smooth flattery and glib eloquence—anything that might confuse the king’s hearing—must not be allowed into his presence. Then his acceptance and rejection will be discerning, and his virtue in listening will be perceptive. Is this not how an enlightened king attends carefully to virtue without?

By settling his intentions through the Way, he prevents desires from sprouting within and thus prepares the foundation for receiving advice. By receiving advice through the Way, he keeps external temptations from entering and further strengthens his ability to maintain his intentions. Such mutual cultivation cannot cease: how, then, could he let his ears and eyes be enslaved and prize exotic objects? Nevertheless, this was merely a man of Lü presenting a mastiff as tribute; we have not heard that King Wu accepted it. Could King Wu have been someone who delighted in flattery and harbored intentions of indulgence? Yet the Duke of Shao’s admonition to settle intentions and receive advice through the Way admitted no delay. Such was the loyal devotion of the great ministers of antiquity. Those in later ages who embellish their words for their own advantage and strive to ingratiate themselves would certainly stand condemned by the Duke of Shao. Yet they must exploit a ruler’s wayward intentions to accomplish this [?]; thus settling one’s intentions is, in turn, the foundation for receiving advice.

The poet recounts how the great general managed military affairs according to the proper Way, thereby showing that he served as a model for all under Heaven. To refrain from exhausting one’s might is a sound guiding principle in warfare. Jifu possessed this virtue: was he not worthy to serve as a model for all under Heaven? 非不可以得志於獫狁也吉甫則以用兵者聖
人所不得已吾惟薄伐以聲其罪而已不必黷
武也大原者天所以限華夷吾惟驅於境外而
已無事窮追也師徒不勤而膚公可奏即是而

translation_en:
… rising at the front, the war chariots were already very steady. As for the horses, they were sturdy and well trained; the four stallions, too, were excellent. With such disciplined troops commanded by so capable a general, success against the Xianyun was certainly possible. Jifu, however, held that warfare was something to which a sage resorted only when compelled: “I need only make a limited attack to proclaim their guilt; there is no need to indulge in warfare.” Taiyuan was the boundary Heaven had set between the Chinese and the foreign peoples: “I need only drive them beyond the border; there is no occasion for pursuing them to the utmost.” Without exhausting his troops, he could report a great achievement. Here Jifu’s comprehensive talents became evident. Could he fail to serve as a model for the myriad states?

In drawing in those who had become estranged and winning over those far away, Jifu’s civil virtues shone forth; in suppressing calamity and settling disorder, his martial prowess inspired awe. Thus, by displaying his civil virtues, he could teach benevolence to all under Heaven. The rulers of the many states who wished to extend policies of pacification and harmony all took him as their model for showing kindness and winning allegiance. Did he merely assist the transforming influence of orderly government? By displaying his martial prowess, he could teach righteousness to all under Heaven. The regional lords and governors who wished to establish achievements of vigorous action all took him as their model for attaining invincibility. Did he merely enhance the might of royal authority?

Ah! This is why Jifu was worthy, and why King Xuan achieved a restoration through him. Even so, although Jifu accomplished the successful northern expedition, King Xuan also brought it about. Had King Xuan not been skilled at appointing generals, even Jifu, worthy though he was, would have had no means of achieving success. Thus King Xuan could restore the accomplishments of Kings Wen and Wu and bring about a restoration because he appointed the worthy and employed the capable. The Book of Changes says, “In the midst of the army: auspicious.” Jifu acted in accordance with this. “Presiding with wisdom: fitting for a great ruler; auspicious.” King Xuan…

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor: “Writers generally fail to examine their material carefully: their work is either prolix or confused. This composition analyzes its subject with precision and clarity, and its language is also dignified. It may be called writing that restores the ancient manner. It should be recorded as a model for the many candidates.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Judge: “In discussing the suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices, its reasoning is clear and its language solemn; its composition is poised and elegant. Finding such a composition in the examination hall could sweep away entrenched bad habits. It should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: “It expresses well the poet’s intention in praising his ruler.”

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent: “Dignified and vigorous.”

The poet praises his ruler for showing reverence at both the suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices and receiving blessings alike from both. Now, these are the great sacrifices of the state. text:
矣今吾君嗣而舉之不有可紀者哉彼其出而
承祀車行則旂建也而交龍之象與輿衛相掩
映矣馬行則轡垂也而六轡之調與驂服相柔
從矣此其明禋之薦雖未之舉而明信之忱則
固已昭也由是而禮行於廟與則順春秋以修
祀罔敢懈焉盡志物以用享罔或過焉若是乎
享親之孝也由是而禮行於郊與則主上帝以
修殷薦崇其報焉配后稷而享騂犧尊其尚焉
若是乎享帝之仁也夫至難格者帝后也吾君
===
仁以事天則馨香上達矣將見是饗是宜而諸
福之物自上錫之也其降福也不既多乎莫難
惠者宗公也吾君孝以事親則精神孚契矣將
見來格來享而繁祉之介若或益之也其福汝
也不亦廣乎吁此固我侯仁孝之應也而亦孰
非臣子之至願哉抑考春秋僖公之世其書曰
禘于太廟用致夫人譏公廟祭之非禮也四卜
郊不從猶三望譏公郊祭之非禮也閟宮之詩
乃侈言其奉祭之福以美之孔子奚取焉噫魯

translation_en:
…indeed. Now that our ruler has succeeded to these rites and performs them, is there nothing worthy of recording? When he goes forth to conduct the sacrifices, his banner is raised as his carriage proceeds, its intertwined dragons setting off the carriages and their guards. As the horses advance, the reins hang down; the six reins are held in harmony, and the outer and inner horses move gently in concert. Although the pure sacrificial offering has yet to be presented, his luminous sincerity and good faith are already manifest. When he then performs the rites in the ancestral temple, he observes the seasons of spring and autumn in conducting the sacrifices, never daring to be remiss. He offers the fullest devotion and material offerings, without any transgression. Such is his filial piety in offering sacrifice to his ancestors! When he performs the rites at the suburban altar, he makes the Lord on High the principal recipient of the grand offering, magnifying his recompense for blessings received. He associates Hou Ji with the sacrifice and offers a reddish bull, honoring the one he reveres. Such is his benevolence in offering sacrifice to the Lord on High!

The Sovereign on High is exceedingly difficult to move; yet when our ruler serves Heaven with benevolence, the fragrant savor rises above. We shall see the offerings accepted and approved, and blessings of every kind bestowed upon him from above. Are the blessings thus sent down not abundant? None are harder to win favor from than the ancestral lords; yet when our ruler serves his ancestors with filial piety, his spirit enters into communion with theirs. We shall see them come and receive the offerings, and abundant blessings bestowed, as though someone were adding still more. Is their blessing of you not far-reaching? Ah! This is surely the response to our lord’s benevolence and filial piety; and which of these blessings is not also the deepest wish of his servants and subjects?

Yet if we examine the Spring and Autumn Annals for the reign of Duke Xi, its record says: “The di sacrifice was performed in the Grand Ancestral Temple, and on this occasion the lady was admitted to the ancestral cult.” This censures the duke’s breach of ritual propriety in the temple sacrifice. “Four divinations were made concerning the suburban sacrifice, but none gave approval; nevertheless, the three sacrifices of distant worship were performed.” This censures the duke’s breach of ritual propriety in the suburban sacrifice. Yet the ode “The Closed Temple” lavishly praises him for the blessings obtained through his sacrifices. What did Confucius find worthy in it? Alas! Lu…

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: “Shows decisive judgment.”

The two hegemons’ employment of worthy ministers is evident in their conduct of warfare and use of strategy. Here, when Zhong obtained control of government, Qi’s military forces were kept within bounds; when Ying presented his plans, Chu’s strength was exhausted. Such were the benefits of employing worthy men for the enterprise of hegemony!

I have heard that employing troops according to established regulations constitutes good military government. A ruler driven solely to exert force will exhaust his people to gratify his ambitions. Duke Huan, however, made Zhong his chief minister, and thereby established domestic administration and military ordinances. Consider his system of gui, li, lian, and xiang units of civil organization, and of wu, rong, zu, and lü military units…

則卑無勞於推轂以師則寡無煩於厚集自是
節制定而財力之賦輕休養成而富彊之業裕
是故召陵徵盟南風弗競矣韓原私搆西顧無
虞矣孰謂一匡之烈非用仲父節兵之效耶故
春秋特稱人於伐宋之役以予其善制云又聞
不戰屈人武之大經也夫唯狃於好勝將奸時
以動矣廼悼也用罃而還師敝楚是圖焉觀其
三分四軍之畫分鋭逆來之算其謀豫矣故兹
===
伐鄭而爲戲之盟也子展有唯強是從之辭而
不校其無信荀偃有圍以待救之策而不許其
力争由是勞心勞力之制明而修德息師之猷
壯是故伯駢請成終必獲鄭矣石𡙇告絶楚將
不能矣孰謂三駕之勳非用武子訏謨所成耶
故春秋特書蕭魚之會於伐鄭盟戲之下以予
其善謀云是可見兵節而時動者威致人而不
致於人者勝齊晉誠得策矣選衆舉賢詢僉從
善知人之哲可誣哉繄紱之臣治於高傒委國

力爭由是勞心勞力之制明而修德息師之猷

其善謀云是可見兵節而時動者威致人而不
致於人者勝齊晉誠得策矣選衆舉賢詢僉從

punctuated:
之規，其制簡矣。故兹伐宋而討北杏貳也，以將則卑，無勞於推轂；以師則寡，無煩於厚集。自是節制定而財力之賦輕，休養成而富彊之業裕。是故召陵徵盟，南風弗競矣；韓原私搆，西顧無虞矣。孰謂一匡之烈，非用仲父節兵之效耶？故《春秋》特稱人於伐宋之役，以予其善制云。
又聞不戰屈人，武之大經也。夫唯狃於好勝，將奸時以動矣。廼悼也用罃，而還師敝楚是圖焉。觀其三分四軍之畫，分鋭逆來之算，其謀豫矣。故兹伐鄭而爲戲之盟也，子展有唯強是從之辭，而不校其無信；荀偃有圍以待救之策，而不許其力争。由是勞心勞力之制明，而修德息師之猷壯。是故伯駢請成，終必獲鄭矣；石𡙇告絶，楚將不能矣。孰謂三駕之勳，非用武子訏謨所成耶？故《春秋》特書蕭魚之會於伐鄭盟戲之下，以予其善謀云。
是可見兵節而時動者威，致人而不致於人者勝，齊晉誠得策矣。選衆舉賢，詢僉從善，知人之哲可誣哉？繄紱之臣治於高傒，委國
translation_en:
…the regulations governing their organization: his arrangements were simple. Thus, when Qi attacked Song to punish its disloyalty to the covenant at Beixing, its commander was of low rank, requiring no elaborate ceremony of dispatch; its troops were few, requiring no burdensome mass mobilization. Thereafter, military discipline was established and levies on wealth and manpower were lightened; recuperation took effect, providing ample scope for building wealth and strength. Thus, when Qi demanded a covenant at Shaoling, the southern power could not contend with it; when the private conflict arose at Hanyuan, Qi had no cause for anxiety to the west. Who could say that the achievement of bringing order to the realm was not the result of employing Father Zhong and exercising restraint in warfare? Hence the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically calls the participants in the campaign against Song “men,” thereby commending the soundness of these arrangements.
I have also heard that subduing others without battle is a cardinal principle of warfare. Those habituated to seeking victory will act in defiance of the proper timing. Duke Dao, however, employed Ying and planned to exhaust Chu by rotating his forces. Consider his plan to divide the four armies into three contingents, and his calculation of dividing his elite troops to meet the enemy’s advance: his strategy was prepared beforehand. Thus, when he attacked Zheng and concluded the covenant at Xi, although Zizhan declared that Zheng would follow only the stronger side, he did not take issue with its untrustworthiness; although Xun Yan proposed besieging Zheng and awaiting its rescuers, he did not permit a contest of force. Consequently, the principle of making some labor with their minds and others with their strength became clear, and the policy of cultivating virtue and resting the troops gained force. Thus, when Bo Pian requested peace, Zheng would ultimately be secured; when Shi [?] announced the severance of relations, Chu would be unable to act. Who could say that the achievement of the three expeditions was not accomplished by employing Wuzi’s grand strategy? Hence the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records the meeting at Xiaoyu after the attack on Zheng and the covenant at Xi, thereby commending the excellence of his strategy.
From this we can see that those who exercise restraint in warfare and act at the proper time command awe, while those who compel others to respond, rather than being compelled by others, achieve victory. Qi and Jin truly obtained sound strategies. Selecting from among the multitude and promoting the worthy, consulting all and following good counsel—could their wisdom in judging men be denied? As for the minister bearing the official ribbon, affairs were managed by Gao Xi [?], and the state was entrusted…

text:
之載書啟以世無相害之盟昭桓公之舊勳申
以謀其不協之望於是齊人知辭順之難犯而
師旋於境矣夫兵車再駕齊怒殆難任也展喜
有辭三軍之氣奪焉若是乎辭之不可以已也
不然室如懸罄其能免於保聚之恐乎以至杞
南許戍秦嘗戍鄭矣巳因掌管之請遂出東門
之師穆之鄙鄭而欲肆封者何如也使鄭而不
慎疆埸之守吾懼桓武之不祀矣幸而高也遇
諸滑郊而遽告焉始以乘韋之先而遠襲之跡
===
彰繼以客館之視而內應之謀敗於是秦人知
有備之難冀而師移於滑矣夫三帥並東秦謀
殆叵測也弦高先覺四境之虞免焉若是乎備
之不可以已也不然超乘三百其何患於攻圍
之不克乎夫觀於修辭可以服暴力不足恃矣
觀于守疆可以破謀詐不足尚矣此王道之所
以貴不戰也長勺之役失之固春秋所深罪與
噫莊固失矣僖鄭亦未得也力罔敵而辭修焉
齊不我逆也迺引豺狼殘親暱無相害之辭安

punctuated: 之載書，啟以世無相害之盟；昭桓公之舊勳，申以謀其不協之望。於是齊人知辭順之難犯，而師旋於境矣。夫兵車再駕，齊怒殆難任也；展喜有辭，三軍之氣奪焉。若是乎辭之不可以已也！不然，室如懸罄，其能免於保聚之恐乎？以至杞南許戍，秦嘗戍鄭矣。巳因掌管之請，遂出東門之師。穆之鄙鄭而欲肆封者何如也！使鄭而不慎疆埸之守，吾懼桓武之不祀矣。幸而高也遇諸滑郊而遽告焉。始以乘韋之先，而遠襲之跡彰；繼以客館之視，而內應之謀敗。於是秦人知有備之難冀，而師移於滑矣。夫三帥並東，秦謀殆叵測也；弦高先覺，四境之虞免焉。若是乎備之不可以已也！不然，超乘三百，其何患於攻圍之不克乎？夫觀於修辭可以服暴，力不足恃矣；觀于守疆可以破謀，詐不足尚矣。此王道之所以貴不戰也。長勺之役失之，固春秋所深罪與？噫！莊固失矣，僖鄭亦未得也。力罔敵而辭修焉，齊不我逆也。迺引豺狼，殘親暱，無相害之辭安
translation_en:
…the covenant document of the former kings, he reminded them of the pledge that their descendants should never harm one another. He proclaimed Duke Huan’s past achievements and reiterated the expectation that he would address discord among the states. Thus the men of Qi recognized how difficult it was to defy such rightful words, and their army turned back at the border. With its war chariots twice dispatched, Qi’s anger was surely hard to withstand; yet Zhan Xi spoke, and the spirit of its entire army was broken. Such is the indispensability of diplomatic speech! Otherwise, with their houses as empty as suspended sounding stones, could the people have escaped the terror of gathering into fortified refuges?

As for “Qi, Nan, Xu, and the garrison” [?], Qin had once stationed troops in Zheng. Then, following a request from those controlling the gates [?], it sent its army out through the eastern gate. How intent Duke Mu was on making Zheng his border territory and extending his domains! Had Zheng not taken care to defend its borders, I fear that sacrifices to Dukes Huan and Wu would have ceased. Fortunately, Xian Gao encountered the troops outside Hua and immediately sent a warning. First, his advance presentation of four hides exposed the distant surprise attack; next, an inspection of the guest quarters thwarted the scheme for assistance from within. The men of Qin then recognized that they could scarcely hope to succeed against a prepared state, and redirected their army toward Hua. With three commanders advancing east together, Qin’s designs were surely unfathomable; yet Xian Gao detected them early, and danger to Zheng’s borders was averted. Such is the indispensability of preparedness! Otherwise, with three hundred men vaulting into their chariots, what reason would Qin have had to fear that its assaults and sieges would fail?

Now, seeing that well-crafted speech can subdue violence, we know that force cannot be relied upon; seeing that guarding the borders can defeat a plot, we know that deceit should not be esteemed. This is why the Kingly Way prizes victory without battle. The battle of Changshao departed from this principle: was this not something the Spring and Autumn Annals deeply condemned? Alas! Duke Zhuang certainly erred, but neither Duke Xi nor Zheng fully attained the right way. Unable to match the enemy’s strength, Duke Xi cultivated diplomatic speech, and Qi did not oppose him. Yet he then enlisted jackals and wolves to ravage his own kin and intimates. Where, then, was the pledge that they should never harm one another …

…When the siege by Qin and Jin became urgent, only then did they seek out Zhu Wu; when the western army secretly approached, it was again Gao who turned it back [?]. What were the meat-eaters—the officials—doing? Thus the kingly Way prizes restraint of desires, and governing a state gives first place to employing worthy men.
Record of Rites
“Music is what the sages delight in, and it can make the people’s hearts good. It moves people deeply and transforms their customs; therefore the former kings established its teaching.”
Wang Zhengyu
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Vice Prefect: Most writers produce prolix accumulations. Classical elegance and outstanding grace, sweeping away all stale habits—this essay alone achieves these qualities. It should be recorded as a model for the many scholars.

The recorder traces the breadth of music’s efficacy and thereby discusses how the sages established their teaching. Music issues from the sage’s heart and moves the hearts of others. How, then, could its teaching fail to be spread throughout the realm? The recorder’s meaning might be expressed thus: People know that music was created to represent virtue, but do they also understand how the former kings used it to make their teaching manifest? Music is not the mere pursuit of sound to its utmost. Because the sage’s virtue accords with the highest degree of centrality and harmony, yet has no means of expression, he gives it voice through rhythm and measure, lending beauty to his feelings of joy. His heart contains the wellspring of sound and vital energy, yet has no means of making it manifest; he therefore gives it form through the movements of dance, to bring forth…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其性天之蘊樂也者非聖人之所樂者乎是樂
也人心之所同也以心感心可以善民心焉夫
人藏其心難乎其感之深也然優柔平中之盛
有以觸天然自有之衷聽之而慾心平躁心釋
焉其感人一何深耶民習異宜難乎其化之速
也然順成和動之休有以妙黎民於變之極聞
之而民風移民俗易焉其化民一何速耶夫樂
之不可以已如此是以先王知天下和平則樂
之道歸焉耳于是以其本之情性者而立之學
===
等以平天下之情凡可以繩德厚者罔不昭示
之也以天下化中生民之道樂為大焉于是以
其稽之度數者而章之聲教以宣天下之化凡
可以象事行者罔不明著之也吁先王之教孰
有大於此者哉雖然樂者感人心之具也而德
者又作樂之本也故曰惟天子建中和之極兼
總條貫金聲而玉振之蓋言本也庶尹允諧舜
之玄德實為之不然鄭衛之音亦音也而何以
其政散其民流耶舉樂者可以有志於本矣
