punctuated: 其性天之蘊。樂也者，非聖人之所樂者乎？是樂也，人心之所同也。以心感心，可以善民心焉。夫人藏其心，難乎其感之深也；然優柔平中之盛，有以觸天然自有之衷，聽之而慾心平、躁心釋焉，其感人一何深耶！民習異宜，難乎其化之速也；然順成和動之休，有以妙黎民於變之極，聞之而民風移、民俗易焉，其化民一何速耶！夫樂之不可以已如此，是以先王知天下和平，則樂之道歸焉耳。于是以其本之情性者，而立之學等，以平天下之情，凡可以繩德厚者，罔不昭示之也。以天下化中，生民之道，樂為大焉。于是以其稽之度數者，而章之聲教，以宣天下之化，凡可以象事行者，罔不明著之也。吁！先王之教，孰有大於此者哉！雖然，樂者感人心之具也，而德者又作樂之本也。故曰：「惟天子建中和之極，兼總條貫，金聲而玉振之。」蓋言本也。庶尹允諧，舜之玄德實為之。不然，鄭衛之音亦音也，而何以其政散、其民流耶？舉樂者可以有志於本矣。
translation_en:
…the depths of his Heaven-endowed nature. Is music not that in which the sage delights? This music is something common to all human hearts. By moving hearts through his own heart, he can make the people's hearts good. People conceal their hearts, so it is difficult to move them deeply. Yet music's fullness of gentleness, serenity, balance, and moderation can touch the inner feelings naturally inherent in them. Hearing it, their desires subside and their agitation dissolves. How profoundly it moves people! The people's accustomed practices differ, so it is difficult to transform them swiftly. Yet the excellence of music's harmonious fulfillment and harmonious movement can wondrously bring the common people to the utmost transformation. Hearing it, their ways change and their customs alter. How swiftly it transforms the people!

Music is thus indispensable. Accordingly, the former kings understood that peace and harmony throughout the world are the ultimate end of the Way of music. They therefore took what was rooted in human feelings and nature and established it in the graded instruction of schools [?], thereby bringing the feelings of all under Heaven into balance. Whatever could regulate and enrich virtue they displayed clearly. In transforming all under Heaven toward the mean [?], music is paramount among the means of guiding the people. They therefore took what was verified against measures and numbers and made it manifest through musical instruction, spreading transformation throughout the world. Whatever could represent affairs and conduct they made plainly apparent. Ah! What aspect of the former kings' teaching could be greater than this?

Nevertheless, music is an instrument for moving people's hearts, while virtue is the foundation for creating music. Thus it is said: “Only the Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of centrality and harmony, comprehensively unites its strands and principles, and brings them together as bells sound at the beginning and jade chimes conclude.” This speaks of the foundation. That the many officials were truly in harmony was in fact the work of Shun's profound virtue. Otherwise, the music of Zheng and Wei was also music; why, then, were their governments disordered and their people wayward? Those who put music into practice should direct their aspirations toward its foundation.

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
是故君子議道自己而置法以民
楊柳
同考試官同知江批理明詞達體裁迥別且善
發君子立教之心足爲矜式録之
考試官右中允張批順暢
考試官右諭德丁批精切
君子以仁爲教論道嚴而立法恕焉蓋道不可
易而法貴宜民也君子欲以仁教天下則所以
明其道行其法者當必有辨矣表記之意若謂
===
仁之難成久矣君子不惟以仁爲己任且將與
民由之其必有以善成其仁乎是故仁之當好
道也安仁者能無欲好之若以爲法而責利仁

translation_en:
“Thus the gentleman takes himself as the starting point in discussing the Way, but takes the people into account in establishing laws.”
Yang Liu
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Vice Prefect: “The reasoning is clear and the language expressive; the composition is markedly distinctive. It also admirably brings out the gentleman’s intention in establishing moral instruction. It deserves to serve as an exemplar. Include it.”
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: “Smooth and fluent.”
Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: “Precise and apt.”
The gentleman makes benevolence the basis of instruction: he is exacting in discussing the Way but considerate in establishing laws. For the Way cannot be altered, whereas laws are valued for their suitability to the people. If the gentleman wishes to instruct all under Heaven through benevolence, he must distinguish between the means of clarifying the Way and those of putting his laws into effect. The meaning of the “Record of Exemplary Conduct” seems to be this: attaining benevolence has long been difficult. The gentleman not only takes benevolence as his own responsibility but also intends to follow it together with the people. Surely he must have a means of successfully bringing their benevolence to fruition!
Thus, that benevolence ought to be loved is a principle of the Way. Those who rest content in benevolence can love it without desire for gain. But if this is made a law and demanded of those who practice benevolence for its benefits, it cannot be put into effect. That what is not benevolent ought to be hated is likewise a principle of the Way. Those who rest content in benevolence can hate it without fear. But if this is made a law and demanded of those who exert themselves to practice benevolence, it cannot be put into effect.
Now the Way has a fixed substance and cannot be lowered. Hence, when the gentleman discusses the Way, he does not shrink from taking his own virtue, brought to its highest perfection, as the standard. In discussing love of benevolence, he necessarily expects it to accord with love free of desire; in discussing hatred of what is not benevolent, he necessarily expects it to arise from hatred free of fear. This is no attempt to force the world into conformity: everything that I ought fully to accomplish is inherent in the Way itself…

translation_en:
…Otherwise, the Way will not be made clear. Methods admit of adaptation and must not be rigidly maintained. Thus, when the gentleman establishes methods, he merely guides people’s inclinations through things they can strive to accomplish. If he wishes the people to love benevolence, he establishes methods of encouragement to show them what is desirable; if he wishes them to hate what is inhumane, he establishes methods that awaken shame to show them what is to be feared. This is no mere accommodation to prevailing customs. To lead the people to do what they must, one should proceed from what they can do; otherwise, the methods will not work. He regards others as himself, grounding his approach in the desire that all should establish themselves and attain fulfillment together. He expects of people what people can achieve, setting forth instructions that are easy to understand and follow. This is the art of benevolence. If, instead, he makes himself the standard for conduct, he will inevitably burden others with demands based on his own abilities. Would the gentleman do this?
Nevertheless, these methods are not devised solely for ordinary people. Even among the great worthies and those below them, attainments differ in degree, and all fall short of resting naturally in benevolence. Thus, when Zigong spoke of bestowing benefits widely, Confucius brought him back to drawing analogies from what lay close at hand. When Zhonggong asked about benevolence, Confucius guided him through reverence and sympathetic understanding: this was still to practice benevolence for its benefits. Overcoming oneself and returning to ritual propriety approaches resting naturally in benevolence, yet it was specifically to Master Yan that he gave this instruction. Such is the variety of methods in teaching! Those who aspire to benevolence may advance from striving to practicing it with ease.

無聲無臭夫語道而歸諸神語載而泯於聲

…the spiritual Way, and the four seasons do not deviate.” Speaking of Heaven, the poet says: “Heaven above has neither sound nor smell.” When speaking of the Way, one attributes it to the spiritual; when speaking of its workings [?], one effaces them in the absence of sound. Heaven’s Way is indeed hidden and subtle. Yet is it not said, “Heaven’s Way extends downward and is □ bright [?]”? Is it not said, “Vast Heaven is bright: it accompanies you when you go forth. Vast Heaven is luminous: it accompanies you when you roam at ease”? Its extending is called extending downward; its brightness is called radiance; going forth and roaming at ease are mentioned. Thus it also embodies all things and is nowhere absent. What is hidden has never failed to be manifest; what is subtle has never failed to be evident. By understanding the manifestation of the hidden and the disclosure of the subtle, one can comprehend Heaven’s Way.

Consider how the sun and moon shine upon us, how the stars stand in dense array, how the four seasons proceed in alternation, how cold and heat succeed one another, how wind and rain spread their moistening influence, how thunder shakes the world, and how frost and snow freeze it hard. None of these is other than Heaven’s teaching; none is other than a means of showing something to humankind. This extends even to the mutual stimulation of closing and opening, movement and stillness; the mutual seeking of floating and sinking, rising and falling; the mutual agitation of victory and defeat, bending and stretching; the intermingling of responses and encounters, gathering and dispersal; and the scattered diversity of dregs, chaff, cinders, and ashes. None of these is other than Heaven’s teaching; none is other than a means of showing something to humankind. Thus it is said: “Not closing off its enduring operation [?]—this is Heaven’s Way. …has a definite substance: it manifests itself without awaiting speech and is not concealed by silence. Thus, although dignified bearing and polished language are manifest, human nature and the Way of Heaven are not obscure either. Although sweeping and cleaning, answering and responding are elementary, refining principles and penetrating the numinous are not profound either. Although filial devotion, brotherly respect, rites, and music are close at hand, fully realizing one’s nature, reaching one’s destiny, fathoming the numinous, and understanding transformation are not remote either. From wholeheartedness and sympathetic understanding, one can infer the single thread that runs through all; from learning what is below, one can attain understanding of what is above; from husband and wife, one can discern Heaven and Earth. It is untenable to say that the sage wishes to conceal this through silence. Why? Because the Way is inherently manifest. The sage, therefore, embodies the Way by which August Heaven constantly displays itself. Since Heaven’s Way conceals nothing, can one say that the sage conceals anything?

Consider how the sage embodies the Way. Warmth, goodness, reverence, frugality, and deference distinguish his bearing; his ease and cheerfulness, respectful candor and assured speech distinguish his demeanor; in his home community, the ancestral temple, and the court, his deportment is properly ordered. This is his embodiment of the Way flowing freely through his limbs. All of it is consummate virtue; all of it serves to show others.

He makes his aspirations clear by bringing ease to the old and cherishing the young. In his choices of calendar, carriage, ceremonial cap, and music, he weighs what is fitting. He makes his achievements manifest by repelling the Lai tribesmen, demolishing the fortifications of the three cities, and securing the return of encroached territory. This is his embodiment of the Way expressed in undertakings. All of it is consummate virtue; all of it serves to show others.

His teaching has distinct aspects: cultural learning, conduct, wholeheartedness, and trustworthiness. He seldom speaks of profit, destiny, and benevolence. He exercises care in giving instruction: he does not enlighten those who are not striving to understand, does not elucidate for those who are not struggling to express themselves, and does not repeat instruction for those unable to infer further from what they have learned. This is his embodiment of the Way appearing in speech and silence. All of it is consummate virtue; all of it serves to show others.

…the Spring and Autumn Annals to rectify names and distinctions of status: this was his embodiment of the Way manifested in compiling and writing. All of it was consummate virtue; all of it served to show others the Way. There were his intentions to go to Gongshan and Bi Xi; his audiences with Yang Huo and Nanzi; his engagement with Chang Ju, Jie Ni, and Jieyu [?]; his tenure as Minister of Justice and acting performance of chief ministerial duties; his taking office when he saw scope for action, when received with propriety, or when supported at public expense; his departures, taking rice still being rinsed or leaving without removing his ceremonial cap; his refusals of Nixi and a ministerial post in Wei; and his joy in resting on his bent arm and eating coarse food. This was his embodiment of the Way manifested in taking office or withdrawing, remaining long or departing quickly. All of it was consummate virtue; all of it served to show others the Way.
Yet the Way embodied in his limbs was entirely one with Heaven’s Way in its illumination from above and its ordered array. The Way embodied in his undertakings was entirely one with Heaven’s Way in its interwoven operations and successive transformations. The Way embodied in his speech and silence was entirely one with Heaven’s Way in its spreading moisture, its thunderous movement, and its stern freezing cold. The Way embodied in his compiling and writing was entirely one with Heaven’s Way in its pervasive radiance [?], its outward movement and unbounded ranging. The Way embodied in his taking office or withdrawing, remaining long or departing quickly, was entirely one with Heaven’s Way: opening and closing, movement and stillness, floating and sinking, rising and falling, prevailing and yielding, bending and stretching, responding and encountering, gathering and dispersing—all mutually affecting and seeking one another, impelling and shaping one another. How fully the sage embodied the Way without concealment, just as Heaven does! Thus it is said: “Heaven’s Way is steadfastly displayed; the sage’s Way is likewise steadfastly displayed.” Only because those who did not know how to learn suspected the sage of concealing something did Confucius himself finally say: “I conceal nothing from you. 知至教之所在矣，聖人體道之情見乎詞矣，學者之疑可以渙然釋矣。雖然，其欲無言者何也？無乃重學者疑畏之心與？是不然也。其曰「天何言哉」，則聖人固以天道示人矣。吾不意聖人以天道示人，而學者習焉不察，猶以有隱致疑也。及門之徒，穎悟莫如賜矣，而猶嘆至道之難聞，是疑聖人體道于深也；悅道如求矣，而顧歉用力之不足，是疑聖人體道于高也。而不知聖道固無隱也。善乎顏子之言曰：「如有所立卓爾。」則聖人無隱之道彰矣。甚矣，顏子之善學也！故為之說曰：「聖人與天為一，顏子與天為徒。」

translation_en:
…one may understand where the highest teaching lies. The sage’s true disposition in embodying the Way is revealed in these words, and learners’ doubts may be entirely dispelled. Yet why did he wish to remain without words? Would this not deepen learners’ doubts and apprehensions? This is not so. When he said, “What does Heaven say?” the sage was indeed showing people the Way of Heaven. I would not have expected that, although the sage showed people the Way of Heaven, learners would grow accustomed to it without examining it, still harboring doubts that he concealed something. Among those who studied under him, none surpassed Ci in perceptiveness; yet even he lamented how difficult it was to hear the supreme Way. This was to suspect that the sage embodied the Way at an inaccessible depth. Qiu delighted in the Way, yet regretted that his strength was insufficient. This was to suspect that the sage embodied the Way at an inaccessible height. They did not understand that the sage’s Way truly concealed nothing. How well Master Yan spoke when he said, “It is as though something stands loftily before me.” Thus the sage’s Way, which conceals nothing, becomes manifest. How accomplished Master Yan was at learning! Hence I offer this explanation: “The sage is one with Heaven; Master Yan is a companion of Heaven.”

On a certain day of a certain month in the fifth year of Chunhua, we reverently received the command establishing an Imperial Diary Office within the palace and appointing your servants Zhouhan and Zong’e to administer the duties of the diarists, qiju lang and qiju sheren.

We humbly reflect that, by opening an office adjoining the jeweled heavens of the imperial residence, you have specially exalted the duties of the two historians. Facing the jade desk, we wet our brushes, thus providing for the compilation of a classic. Since the office lies beside the secluded inner precincts, its responsibilities should be entrusted to men selected for talent and virtue. Who could have imagined that ordinary men such as ourselves would undeservedly receive your gracious command? Your servants Zhouhan and the others, in profound fear and trembling, bow our heads and knock them upon the ground, submitting these words:

We humbly consider that the duties of the Imperial Diary Office originate in the established practices of the Historiographers of the Left and Right. They recorded words and actions to instruct posterity, attaching dates and times to transmit a trustworthy account. The Han dynasty had diaries, apparently compiled by palace historians; from the Jin onward, close attendants of the ruler were regularly assigned concurrent responsibility for them. Through successive dynasties there was still no dedicated official. Only under the Later Wei were personnel appointed for this purpose, and the Northern Qi followed this precedent by establishing a department. When the institutional arrangements of the Sui and Tang had become fully developed, the posts of qiju lang and qiju sheren were first distinguished. Their offices were separately assigned beside the palace precincts, and both ranked among the imperial attendants at Ganquan. Attending at the hollow beneath the carved dragon of the palace steps, they recorded events, thereby furnishing material for the Grand Astrologer’s extensive knowledge. Yet the inherited practice grew increasingly remote from that of the Three Exemplary Sovereigns, and its surviving precedents were almost obliterated during the Five Dynasties.

translation_en:
…When the illustrious dynasty was first established, its institutional arrangements underwent some revision. Personnel were attached to the Secretariat and Chancellery, and the office fortunately found a place there. Its offices were arrayed in the outer court, but the circulation of imperial commands amounted merely to formal communication [?]; its titles became empty designations carrying stipends, and the original purpose of establishing the office was lost. With the imperial residence so distant, what became of the intention to accord the office an honored place within the palace? Daily records were heard of in name alone; the practice of recording events had long fallen into disuse. To put into effect the excellent institutions of a sovereign's reign, the omissions accumulated over successive generations had to be made good. The imperial institutions were renewed, and the regular duties of officials were set right.
This was because we humbly encountered Your Majesty, who receives Heaven's mandate and holds the register of sovereign succession, wielding the celestial symbols to rule the people. You issue words like silken cords and stout ropes, and establish the supreme standard in conformity with compass and square. Your sagacious plans order military affairs, unifying carriage gauges and writing across ten thousand li; your profound strategies give civil culture its pattern, reviving the rites and music of a hundred years. You immerse your mind in the canonical writings and bring the world to music and song [?], pursuing the admirable customs of pristine antiquity and perfecting the magnificent spectacle of great peace. You therefore accepted the petition of your officials and enhanced the standing of the officials charged with keeping the imperial diary. You moved their office into the secluded and solemn palace precincts, having them share duty in the imperial and Hanlin quarters; you welcomed worthy men into confidential service to compose accounts worthy of preservation in jade cases and golden coffers. These encompass every utterance and action of the sovereign and every governmental command concerning the various offices, reaching upward to the full range of celestial phenomena and downward to the entire terrestrial realm…

punctuated: 内而民俗之澆醇，外而裔夷之逆順，典章制度折衷考古之規，食貨兵刑損益趨時之用。或日報，或月報，或歲報，謨猷克集於盈庭；為大書，為特書，為屢書，義例俱存於授簡。藏之石渠之署，彝憲足徵；付之金馬之庭，著作有據。亶云重任，端賴名儒。如臣等猥以譾材，謬塵華貫，握丹鉛於史局，宐兼五志之長；探緗素於書林，靡摠九流之要。顧濫吹之已久，慮策蹇之難前。豈期内史之新銜，復荷大君之異數！上林借寵，知附鳳之暉遥；下里裁歌，柰雕蟲之技盡！志非幾於微婉，責以屬辭；文罔及於贍詳，俾之敘事。何以述朝廷之駿烈？何以揚明聖之鴻休？遊聖人門，實有難言之懼；代大匠斲，更深傷指之慙。臣等敢不勉竭虚庸，務遵實錄，辨不華，質不俚，發凡開柱下之編，退補過，進盡忠，托始載
translation_en:
…within the realm, the corruption or integrity of popular customs; beyond it, the defiance or submission of distant peoples. Statutes and institutions are assessed against standards drawn from antiquity; food supply, finance, military affairs, and punishments are adjusted to meet the needs of the times. Through reports submitted daily, monthly, or yearly, plans and counsels are assembled from the officials filling the court. Whether matters receive prominent entry, special entry, or repeated entry, the principles governing their recording are preserved when the writing tablets are entrusted to the historians. Stored in the Shiqu archives, these records provide evidence of enduring norms; delivered to the court of the Golden Horse Gate, they furnish a basis for historical composition. Truly this is a weighty responsibility, dependent above all upon eminent scholars.
Men such as your servants, with our paltry abilities, have undeservedly occupied distinguished ranks. Wielding vermilion and lead at the Historiography Office, we ought to unite the strengths of the five aims [?]; searching the silk-bound volumes in the forest of books, we have failed to grasp the essentials of the Nine Schools. We reflect that we have long passed ourselves off as capable, like an incompetent musician in an ensemble, and fear that, like a lame horse urged onward, we can scarcely advance. How could we have expected this new designation as court historians, or to receive once again such exceptional favor from our sovereign?
Borrowing favor in the Shanglin imperial park, we know how distant is the radiance of the phoenix to which we cling. Composing a rustic song, what can we do when our petty literary skill is exhausted? Our understanding falls short of subtlety and delicacy, yet we are charged with composing the text; our writing cannot attain fullness and detail, yet we are made to narrate events. How can we recount the court’s magnificent achievements? How can we proclaim the vast blessings of our enlightened sage ruler? Entering the sage’s gate, we truly fear the difficulty of speaking worthily; wielding the adze in place of a master carpenter, we feel still deeper shame at injuring our fingers.
How could your servants dare not strive to exhaust our meager abilities and diligently adhere to truthful recording? Discriminating without ornament, plain without vulgarity, we shall establish the guiding principles and commence the compilation befitting the Keeper of the Archives. In retirement we shall remedy our faults; in service we shall devote our utmost loyalty. Taking this as our starting point, we shall record …

This answer expounds its responses clearly and fully, and its praise is fitting. At the end it returns earnestly to proposals for study through lectures and the presentation of counsel, drawing substantively on the teachings of Yi Yin and Shao. Does its author harbor a heart of devoted loyalty?

Comment by Associate Examiner Song, Department Magistrate: The plans and teachings of our imperial ancestors are inexhaustible, and the principles of governing the mind and emulating the ancestors are especially fully set forth in the Four Books. These are truly enduring standards for their sagely sons and divine descendants. This policy essay excels in elucidating them clearly and exhaustively. Moreover, it expresses hopes for the presentation of lectures and counsel. Does its author also understand the essentials of transmitting the mind through sagely learning?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Prefectural Judge: The Four Books imperially composed by our ancestors truly continue the ancient transmission of sagely learning from the emperors and kings of antiquity. They provide enduring standards by which their sagely sons and divine descendants may govern their minds and emulate their ancestors. This answer expounds its responses clearly and comprehensively, and offers praise skillfully. At its close it again expresses great earnestness concerning proposals for the presentation of lectures and counsel. Does its author also revere the virtue of the imperial ancestors and harbor the loyalty of Yi Yin and Fu Yue?

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: The plans and teachings bequeathed by our imperial ancestors, which serve as enduring standards for their sagely sons and divine descendants, are all contained in the Four Books. You have comprehended their essential principles and presented proposals for lectures and counsel, with earnest and deeply felt language and intent. You seem to aspire to exalt □□ [?]—cause for rejoicing at having obtained a worthy scholar.

The learning of a ruler has an essential task: governing the mind. It also has a standard: modeling oneself upon one’s ancestors. Through governing the mind, the ruler’s resolve becomes settled and order throughout the realm is achieved. Through modeling himself upon his ancestors, he closely follows their example and puts into practice the way of adhering to their precedents. Surely it is entirely through these that a ruler attains principle through ease and simplicity and takes his place between Heaven and Earth! title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
惟精惟一允執厥中是舜以所得統於堯
者而命之禹也先儒謂唐虞授受開萬世
心學之原不以此耶嗣是而禹得統於舜
則儉勤祗德惡酒好言禹之所以入聖者
此學也湯得統於禹則不邇不殖懋昭大
德湯之所以反身者此學也文武得統於
湯則亦臨亦保不泄不忘緝熈敬止建其
有極文武之所以丕顯丕承者此學也所
謂相授守一道非耶三代以降如漢高之
===
不事詩書文帝之專尚黃老固不足以語
於務學之急而唐宗之討論經籍宋君之
日呈御覽亦何足以語於正心之要也求
其庶幾於古帝王之心學者不亦鮮哉洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝開天立極即位之初首著
祖訓一書以貽孫謀以昭燕翼焉是書也有曰
持守也嚴祭祀也謹出入慎國政也則治
道之大綱也有曰禮儀也律法也內命職

…Be discerning, be single-minded, and faithfully hold to the mean. Thus Shun charged Yu with the tradition of rule he had received from Yao. Earlier Confucian scholars said that the transmission between Yao and Shun opened the source of the learning of the mind for all generations. Was this not why? Thereafter, Yu received the tradition from Shun: he was frugal and diligent, reverenced virtue, shunned wine, and welcomed good counsel. It was through this learning that Yu attained sagehood. Tang received the tradition from Yu: he did not approach sensual pleasures or accumulate wealth, and he strove to manifest great virtue. It was through this learning that Tang examined himself. Kings Wen and Wu received the tradition from Tang: they watched over and protected their people, neither slackening nor forgetting, continually made reverence shine forth, and established the supreme standard. It was through this learning that Wen and Wu gloriously manifested and grandly carried on their inheritance. Is this not what is meant by transmitting to one another and preserving a single Way?
After the Three Dynasties, such examples as Gaozu of Han’s neglect of the Odes and Documents and Emperor Wen’s exclusive esteem for the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi certainly fall short of what is meant by making learning an urgent priority. Yet how could the Tang emperor’s discussions of the classics or the daily presentation of texts for the Song ruler’s inspection suffice to express the essential task of rectifying the mind? Were not those who came anywhere near the ancient sage-kings’ learning of the mind exceedingly few?
We reverently consider how our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new order and established the supreme standard. At the beginning of his reign, he first composed the Ancestral Instructions, laying plans for his descendants and making clear his provision for their security. This book speaks of maintaining oneself, solemnizing sacrifices, exercising care in going out and coming in, and attending circumspectly to affairs of state: these are the great guiding principles of governance. It also speaks of ritual observances, laws, and the offices appointed within the palace…

忠勤也廉謹也此臣道之大者也三王之

文華大訓一書語其綱則首之以進學次之
以養德又次之以厚倫又次之以明治也
語其要則務學爲要矣養德以之厚倫以
之明治以之也此又非大訓之綱要乎是
四書者大義垂示固已炳若日星矣由今

祖宗而不惑可也謂我

其心同其學同耶夫

…Emperor Xianzong Chun, continuing an era of brilliance and peace, once compiled a book entitled Great Instructions of the Hall of Literary Brilliance (Wenhua daxun) in the time remaining from affairs of state. As for its essentials, dedication to learning is foremost: through it virtue is cultivated, human relationships are strengthened, and governance is clarified. Are these not, in turn, the framework and essentials of the Great Instructions? The great principles that these four books have transmitted for posterity are already as radiant as the sun and stars. The teachings on strengthening human relationships and clarifying governance embody Emperor Shun’s discernment of human relationships and understanding of things. punctuated:
□宗之發端，爲聖子神孫發也。況祖述者不若憲章之爲切，遠宗者不若近守之爲真。率由祖宗，其則不遠。故本之祖訓以求其端，則所謂持守者不可已也；攷之精誠以致其實，則所謂無妄者不可忽也；正之心法以大其規，則所謂學問者不可緩也；欽之大訓以要其止，則所謂養德者不可後也。非聖學緝熈之一助耶？

至於經筵之定於文華也，有由矣。國初經筵無定日，亦無定所。無定日，則無時非學也；無定所，則無處非學也。當時燕息所止，皆講學之地；侍從所接，皆講學之臣。自正統以來，始定於文華殿，豈以學貴專一，知止有定耶？累朝因之，無容喙矣。頃言者有陳講畢進言之
translation_en:
…□zong’s [?] inauguration of this was undertaken for his sagely sons and divine grandsons. Moreover, tracing and transmitting ancient models is less directly pertinent than following established precedents; taking distant predecessors as models is less concrete than adhering to those nearer at hand. Follow the imperial ancestors: the standard is not far away. Thus, if one takes the Ancestral Instructions as the foundation for seeking its beginnings, what is called steadfast adherence must never cease. If one examines it through wholehearted sincerity to give it substance, what is called freedom from falsity must not be neglected. If one rectifies it through the teachings on the mind to enlarge its scope, what is called learning and inquiry must not be delayed. If one reveres the Great Instructions to grasp its ultimate goal, what is called nurturing virtue must not be put last. Would this not assist the continuing illumination of Your Majesty’s sagely learning?

As for the fixing of the Classics Colloquium at Wenhua Hall, there was a reason for it. At the beginning of the dynasty, the Classics Colloquium had neither fixed days nor a fixed location. With no fixed days, there was no time that was not a time for learning; with no fixed location, there was no place that was not a place for learning. In those days, wherever the emperor rested at leisure was a place for expounding learning, and all the attendant officials he received were ministers who expounded learning. Only from the Zhengtong reign onward was its location fixed at Wenhua Hall. Was this because learning prizes single-minded concentration, and knowing the goal gives one settled purpose? Successive reigns followed this practice, and there is no room to dispute it. Recently, among those submitting advice, someone has presented a proposal for offering counsel after the lecture has concluded…

translation_en:
…a proposal to offer counsel after the lectures. I, this humble student, believe that it must not be dismissed as impractical and left unimplemented. In the age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, when a minister spoke, the ruler assented; when the ruler spoke, a minister could voice dissent. The sovereign as head and the ministers as limbs truly formed a single body. In later ages, the distinction between the throne and the steps below became forbiddingly strict, and ruler and ministers were separated by ceremonial barriers. Thus the spirit of joyful cooperation in undertaking their duties became remote and unheard of. Now the Classics Colloquium is held, and Your Majesty’s sacred learning flourishes; yet beyond the lectures and readings, no one offers a word. The sources of success and failure in government, the causes of the people’s well-being and distress, the distinction between upright and corrupt character, and the incipient causes of order and disorder, past and present—the attendant ministers dare not speak of these, and so there are matters the sovereign does not hear about. This proposal to offer counsel must therefore be put into practice.

This is no mere conjecture. During the Hongzhi reign, after the Classics Colloquium lectures, the Grand Secretaries were summoned to return to Wenhua Hall to examine memorials together with the emperor. Our Emperor Jing personally followed this practice. During the Hongwu reign, an instruction was issued to the officials responsible for lecturing and reading: “Although those serving in the Hanlin Academy have deliberation and reflection as their duties, you are already numbered among my close attendants and are at my side morning and evening. Concerning successes and failures in the government of the realm, and benefits and harms to the people, you must speak of everything you know.” Our Emperor Gao thus instructed his ministers.

Yi Yin’s Instruction says: “The succeeding king has newly received his…”

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
命惟新厥德終始惟一時乃日新召公之誥
曰若生子罔不在厥初生自貽哲命則匡
聖學而成
主德執事事也執事責也愚生何足與知之哉
謹對
第二問
王正宇
同考試官同知江批學識洞微議論正大且於
士習吏治推原轉移化導之本足為返古還淳之助喬薦允宜
===

於挽時起敝之要尤能諤諤言之蓋士之學古而適用者取之

之士鮮忠朴燕趙之士寡深沉所以移之

translation_en:
…the mandate, renew your virtue. Remain constant from beginning to end, and thus renew yourself daily.” The Duke of Shao’s admonition says: “As with the birth of a child, everything depends upon its first beginnings; secure for yourself a wise destiny.” Thus, to guide His Majesty’s learning and perfect the ruler’s virtue is your task and your responsibility, gentlemen. How could an ignorant student such as I presume to understand these matters? Respectfully submitted.

Second Policy Question
Wang Zhengyu

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Vice Prefect: “His learning and understanding penetrate subtleties, and his arguments are upright and sound. Moreover, in discussing the habits of scholars and the conduct of officials, he traces the foundations of transformation and moral guidance. This can help restore ancient ways and simple integrity. Qiao’s recommendation [?] is entirely fitting.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Right Assistant Mentor: “His systematic analysis of the habits of scholars and the conduct of officials under the Han is clear in every detail. On the essentials of rescuing the age and remedying its failings, he speaks with particular forthrightness. Here is a scholar who studies antiquity and applies it to practical affairs. Accept him.”

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Exhorter: “His answers concerning the habits of scholars and the conduct of officials under the two Han dynasties are systematic and omit nothing. His concluding remarks on remedying abuses are especially well directed at the maladies of our time. This is someone with aspirations to bring order to the world. Select him.”

That the habits of scholars and the conduct of officials flourished in antiquity resulted from those above taking the lead. That they have deteriorated today results from the transforming influence of prevailing trends. What those above establish provides a standard for those below; wherever prevailing influences sweep, the customary preferences of the age shift accordingly. Thus, scholars of Zou and Lu seldom possessed loyalty and simplicity [?], while scholars of Yan and Zhao seldom possessed depth and reserve: the influences that transformed them differed. Officials of the Zhou esteemed integrity and competence, while officials of the tyrannical Qin prized severity…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
苛所以作之者殊也知此則率作興事之
機起弊維風之術有經世之責者可以加
之意矣請因明問而陳之蓋聞三五之世
道德一而風俗同士習純而吏治美粹乎
無以議矣三代以還惟漢去古未遠故先
儒之言士習者曰西漢尚經術東漢崇節
義也史臣稽吏治者曰漢世良吏為盛也
謂近古非與粤昔西漢之興孝惠除挾書
之禁武皇表六籍之微勸學興禮為天下
===
先一時挾策談經彬彬然多文學之士矣
人見京房之於易伏勝孔安國之於書匡
衡之於詩仲舒之於春秋后蒼之於禮也
遂以經術歸之然攷其時以節義表著者
未嘗不數數然也故直諫守節不有寢淮
南之謀如汲黯者乎持節虜庭不有牧漠
北之羝如蘇武者乎不有借劔尚方如朱
雲者乎不有耻就吏治如蕭望之者乎他
如龔勝之不受印綬也薛方之托迹巢由

punctuated: 苛，所以作之者殊也。知此，則率作興事之機、起弊維風之術，有經世之責者可以加之意矣。請因明問而陳之。蓋聞三五之世，道德一而風俗同，士習純而吏治美，粹乎無以議矣。三代以還，惟漢去古未遠。故先儒之言士習者曰：「西漢尚經術，東漢崇節義也。」史臣稽吏治者曰：「漢世良吏為盛也。」謂近古，非與？粤昔西漢之興，孝惠除挾書之禁，武皇表六籍之微，勸學興禮，為天下先。一時挾策談經，彬彬然多文學之士矣。人見京房之於易，伏勝、孔安國之於書，匡衡之於詩，仲舒之於春秋，后蒼之於禮也，遂以經術歸之。然攷其時，以節義表著者，未嘗不數數然也。故直諫守節，不有寢淮南之謀如汲黯者乎？持節虜庭，不有牧漠北之羝如蘇武者乎？不有借劔尚方如朱雲者乎？不有耻就吏治如蕭望之者乎？他如龔勝之不受印綬也，薛方之托迹巢由
translation_en:
…harshness: this was because those who shaped their conduct differed. Understanding this, those responsible for governing the realm may give thought to the means of leading men into action and undertaking affairs, and to the arts of remedying abuses and sustaining proper customs. Allow me to elaborate in response to your illuminating question. I have heard that in the age of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, the Way and virtue were one and customs were uniform; scholars’ habits were pure and official administration excellent—so flawless that nothing could be criticized. Since the Three Dynasties, only the Han remained close to antiquity. Thus earlier Confucian scholars, speaking of scholars’ habits, said: “The Western Han esteemed classical learning; the Eastern Han revered integrity and righteousness.” Historiographers, examining official administration, said: “Good officials flourished most abundantly under the Han.” Is it not right to call it close to antiquity?

When the Western Han arose, Emperor Xiaohui abolished the prohibition on possessing books, and Emperor Wu brought to light the subtle meanings of the Six Classics. They encouraged learning and promoted ritual, setting an example for the realm. In those days, men carried books and discussed the classics; scholars of refined literary learning were plentiful. People observed Jing Fang’s work on the Changes, Fu Sheng’s and Kong Anguo’s on the Documents, Kuang Heng’s on the Odes, Zhongshu’s on the Spring and Autumn Annals, and Hou Cang’s on ritual, and consequently characterized the age by its classical learning. Yet if we examine that time, men distinguished by integrity and righteousness were also repeatedly to be found. Among those who remonstrated frankly and upheld their principles, was there not Ji An, whose presence thwarted the conspiracy of Huainan? Among those who retained their envoy’s credentials at the barbarians’ court, was there not Su Wu, who tended rams north of the desert? Was there not Zhu Yun, who requested the sword of the Imperial Manufactories Office? Was there not Xiao Wangzhi, who deemed it shameful to submit to judicial officials? Other examples include Gong Sheng’s refusal to accept the seal and ribbon of office, and Xue Fang’s taking Chao Fu and Xu You as models for his withdrawal…

text:
也之數子者勁節直道確乎不渝謂無得
於節義可乎如是而曰專尚經術不已偏
耶東漢之興光武切幽人之徵嚴光厲高
尚之節逸民一舉天下歸心一時激論危
言凛凛乎多忠憤之士矣人見膺之獨持
風裁蕃之不畏彊禦密之達賢糾惡滂之
慨然攬轡皇甫規之耻不與黨也遂以節
義歸之然攷其時以經術著稱者未嘗不
比比然也故篤信好古不有如伏湛者乎
===
徧習五經不有如桓譚者乎不有囊括大
典如鄭玄者乎不有刪定公羊嚴氏春秋
如樊儵者乎他如馬融之名重關西也蔡
邕之正訂五經也之數子者博物洽聞為
世推服謂無得於經術可乎如是而曰專
崇節義不已拘耶是知經術尚矣而節義
亦無不崇言西漢之士者此其大準也若
乃諛佞成風至有借六藝以文奸者謂之
見道不明則可遂以是為經術病焉亦奚

比比然也故篤信好古不有如伏湛者乎
===
徧習五經不有如桓譚者乎不有囊括大
典如鄭玄者乎不有刪定公羊嚴氏春秋
如樊儵者乎他如馬融之名重關西也蔡
邕之正訂五經也之數子者博物洽聞爲
世推服謂無得於經術可乎如是而曰專
崇節義不已拘耶是知經術尚矣而節義
亦無不崇言西漢之士者此其大凖也若
乃諛佞成風至有借六藝以文奸者謂之
見道不明則可遂以是爲經術病焉亦奚
punctuated:
也。之數子者，勁節直道，確乎不渝，謂無得於節義可乎？如是而曰專尚經術，不已偏耶？東漢之興，光武切幽人之徵，嚴光厲高尚之節，逸民一舉，天下歸心，一時激論危言，凛凛乎多忠憤之士矣。人見膺之獨持風裁，蕃之不畏彊禦，密之達賢糾惡，滂之慨然攬轡，皇甫規之耻不與黨也，遂以節義歸之。然攷其時，以經術著稱者，未嘗不比比然也。故篤信好古，不有如伏湛者乎？徧習五經，不有如桓譚者乎？不有囊括大典如鄭玄者乎？不有刪定公羊嚴氏春秋如樊儵者乎？他如馬融之名重關西也，蔡邕之正訂五經也，之數子者，博物洽聞，為世推服，謂無得於經術可乎？如是而曰專崇節義，不已拘耶？
是知經術尚矣，而節義亦無不崇，言西漢之士者，此其大準也。若乃諛佞成風，至有借六藝以文奸者，謂之見道不明則可，遂以是為經術病焉，亦奚
translation_en:
…These men maintained firm integrity and an upright course, steadfast and unchanging. Can one say that they attained nothing in moral integrity and righteousness? Given this, is it not one-sided to say that they esteemed only classical learning? When the Eastern Han arose, Emperor Guangwu earnestly sought to summon recluses to service, while Yan Guang upheld his lofty resolve. With this single act concerning a recluse, the hearts of all under Heaven turned toward the dynasty. In that age, impassioned argument and fearless speech abounded: there were many awe-inspiring men filled with loyal indignation. People observe how Li Ying alone upheld exacting moral standards, how Chen Fan did not fear the powerful, how Mi [?] advanced the worthy and censured the wicked, how Fan Pang resolutely took up the reins, and how Huangfu Gui felt ashamed not to be counted among the proscribed partisans. They consequently characterize these men in terms of moral integrity and righteousness. Yet examination of that age shows that men renowned for classical learning were also everywhere to be found. For steadfast faith and love of antiquity, was there not Fu Zhan? For comprehensive study of the Five Classics, was there not Huan Tan? Was there not Zheng Xuan, who encompassed the great canonical writings in his learning? Was there not Fan Shu, who edited and established the text of the Yan school’s Gongyang tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals? Other examples include Ma Rong, whose reputation carried great weight west of the passes, and Cai Yong, who corrected and established the texts of the Five Classics. These men possessed extensive knowledge and comprehensive learning, and won the admiration and respect of their age. Can one say that they attained nothing in classical learning? Given this, is it not unduly restrictive to say that they honored only moral integrity and righteousness?
Thus we know that classical learning was esteemed, while moral integrity and righteousness were likewise universally honored. This is the broad standard for discussing the scholars of the Western Han. As for flattery and obsequiousness becoming fashionable, to the point that some even borrowed the Six Arts to cloak their wickedness, one may say that their understanding of the Way was unclear. But to take this as a fault of classical learning itself—how could that…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
可哉節義崇矣而經術亦無不尚言東漢
之士者此其大較也若乃噓枯吹生至有
甘危言以就戮者謂之明哲未至則然遂
以是爲節義病焉豈其然哉然則三代而
下語士習之近古者惟漢其庶幾乎至若
傳西京之循吏者班固也則有若文翁也
王成也黃霸朱邑也龔遂召信臣也皆守
也令長于時不少概見豈西京之治令有
未循與是有說也蓋西漢稱良吏之盛者
===
宣帝爲最夷攷宣帝繇側陋而登至尊知
民事之艱難是以躬親萬幾厲精圖治謂
吏民之本者太守也而不言夫令也親見
臨問觀所由而察所行者刺史守相也而
不及夫令也謂與我共治而有璽書之褒
金秩之寵者二千石也而不與夫令也入
爲九卿徵爲少府賜爵關內侯者郡守也
而令不逮也宣帝知郡守之職其任爲甚
重而不知縣令之職於民爲最親令長之

可哉？節義崇矣，而經術亦無不尚，言東漢之士者，此其大較也。若乃噓枯吹生，至有甘危言以就戮者，謂之明哲未至則然，遂以是爲節義病焉，豈其然哉？然則三代而下，語士習之近古者，惟漢其庶幾乎！

至若傳西京之循吏者，班固也。則有若文翁也，王成也，黃霸、朱邑也，龔遂、召信臣也，皆守也。令長于時不少，概見豈西京之治，令有未循與？是有說也。蓋西漢稱良吏之盛者，宣帝爲最。夷攷宣帝繇側陋而登至尊，知民事之艱難，是以躬親萬幾，厲精圖治。謂吏民之本者太守也，而不言夫令也；親見臨問，觀所由而察所行者，刺史、守、相也，而不及夫令也；謂與我共治，而有璽書之褒、金秩之寵者，二千石也，而不與夫令也；入爲九卿，徵爲少府，賜爵關內侯者，郡守也，而令不逮也。宣帝知郡守之職，其任爲甚重，而不知縣令之職，於民爲最親。令長之
translation_en:
…how could that be acceptable? Integrity and righteousness were exalted, yet classical learning was also universally esteemed: this is the broad outline for those discussing the scholars of the Eastern Han. As for those whose praise and blame could wither or revive reputations, some went so far as willingly to speak perilously forthright words and meet execution. To say that they fell short of discerning wisdom would be justified; but could one therefore regard this as a defect in integrity and righteousness? Thus, after the Three Dynasties, if we speak of scholarly conduct approaching that of antiquity, surely the Han came closest!

As for the man who wrote biographies of the conscientious officials of the Western Capital, it was Ban Gu. Those included were Wen Weng, Wang Cheng, Huang Ba, Zhu Yi, Gong Sui, and Shao Xinchen—all commandery governors. County magistrates were not few at the time; does this general picture suggest that, under Western Han rule, the magistrates were not conscientious [?]? There is an explanation. Among Western Han reigns celebrated for an abundance of good officials, Emperor Xuan’s was foremost. On examining [?] how Emperor Xuan rose from humble obscurity to the supreme position, we find that he understood the hardships of the people’s affairs. He therefore personally attended to the myriad affairs of state and exerted himself to achieve good government. He declared that commandery governors were the foundation for officials and people, but did not mention county magistrates. Those whom he received and questioned personally, observing their methods and examining their conduct, were regional inspectors, commandery governors, and kingdom chancellors; county magistrates were not included. Those of whom he said, “They govern jointly with me,” and whom he favored with commendations in sealed imperial letters, gold, and official rank, were officials of two thousand bushels; county magistrates did not share in these favors. Those brought into the central government as one of the Nine Chamberlains, summoned to serve as Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues, or granted the rank of Marquis within the Passes were commandery governors; county magistrates did not attain such honors. Emperor Xuan knew that the responsibilities of commandery governors were exceedingly weighty, but did not recognize that the office of county magistrate was closest to the people. As for the county magistrates’…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
所以不聞於時者不以上之所崇重者自
有在耶至若傳東京之循吏者范曄也則
有如衞颯也王渙也孟嘗第五訪也劉矩
劉寵仇香童恢也皆令長也而郡守不多
述焉豈東京之治令長爲獨盛與又有說
也蓋東漢號循吏之盛者光武爲最更攷
光武長於民間頗達情偽是以廣求民瘼
觀納風謠方崎嶇兵革卓茂以仁愛聞則
擢而寘之羣公之右固不以密令之微而
===
有所輕也祭彤以清政顯則增秩賜縑以
為之勸亦不以襄賁之小而有所忽也謡
言單辭必為轉易非輕於去取也慮夫用
匪其人或以為民之害也四百餘縣悉從
減省非輕於更易也慮夫浮費冗食徒以
為民之擾也帝之於令審重如此是以出
宰百里皆以郎官令長之所以章章著聞
者不以上之所重在此耶若乃以能著于
西京者若趙廣漢張敞之輩非不赫然稱

punctuated: 所以不聞於時者，不以上之所崇重者自有在耶？至若傳東京之循吏者，范曄也，則有如衞颯也、王渙也、孟嘗、第五訪也、劉矩、劉寵、仇香、童恢也，皆令長也，而郡守不多述焉。豈東京之治，令長爲獨盛與？又有說也。蓋東漢號循吏之盛者，光武爲最。更攷光武長於民間，頗達情偽，是以廣求民瘼，觀納風謠。方崎嶇兵革，卓茂以仁愛聞，則擢而寘之羣公之右，固不以密令之微而有所輕也。祭彤以清政顯，則增秩賜縑，以為之勸，亦不以襄賁之小而有所忽也。謡言單辭，必為轉易，非輕於去取也，慮夫用匪其人，或以為民之害也。四百餘縣，悉從減省，非輕於更易也，慮夫浮費冗食，徒以為民之擾也。帝之於令，審重如此，是以出宰百里，皆以郎官。令長之所以章章著聞者，不以上之所重在此耶？若乃以能著于西京者，若趙廣漢、張敞之輩，非不赫然稱
translation_en: …the reason they went unheard of in their own time—was it not that those above reserved their esteem for others? As for Fan Ye, who wrote the biographies of the conscientious officials of the Eastern Han, he included such men as Wei Sa, Wang Huan, Meng Chang, Diwu Fang, Liu Ju, Liu Chong, Qiu Xiang, and Tong Hui. All were county magistrates or chiefs, whereas he recorded few commandery governors. Could it be that, under Eastern Han rule, county magistrates and chiefs alone flourished? There is another explanation. Among Eastern Han reigns renowned for their abundance of conscientious officials, Guangwu’s was foremost. Examining further, we find that Guangwu grew up among the common people and understood well what was genuine and what was false. He therefore sought widely to learn of the people’s sufferings and examined and heeded their folk songs. Even while struggling amid warfare, when Zhuo Mao became known for benevolence and kindness, he promoted him above all the highest dignitaries. He certainly did not slight him because of his humble position as Magistrate of Mi. When Ji Tong became distinguished for incorrupt administration, he increased his salary rank and bestowed fine silk upon him as encouragement; nor did he overlook him because Xiangben was a small county. On hearing a popular report or even a single statement, he would make a change in appointments. This was not carelessness in dismissing or retaining officials: he feared that employing the wrong person might harm the people. He reduced or abolished more than four hundred counties. This was not carelessness in making changes: he feared that needless expenditure and superfluous salaried personnel would merely burden the people. Such was the Emperor’s care and seriousness concerning county magistrates that all those sent out to govern a county were selected from the Gentlemen at court. Was not the conspicuous renown of county magistrates and chiefs due to the importance those above attached to them? As for those renowned for ability under the Western Han, men such as Zhao Guanghan and Zhang Chang, it was certainly not that they lacked illustrious acclaim…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
信也然專任刑罰而終抵罪誅視康廉德
讓之風有餘愧焉其不載之循吏者固非
無見也以能著於東京者若邊鳳延篤之
儔非不卓然稱能也然比迹趙張而政多
深刻視道德齊禮之治有不逮焉其不載
之循吏者曄非無見也然則三代而下語
吏治之近古者惟漢其庶幾乎至於今之
士習吏治則誠有可太息者焉以士習言
之工藝文者富靡麗之虛詞其流入于支
===
蔓而無實談性命者拾良知之餘緒其究
入於禪伯而無歸孔子所謂言有枝葉此
其人也執事以為日漓誠漓矣以吏治言
之習理財者牟利秋毫以督租辦課為有
用立刑威者用刑次骨以搏姦擊彊為已
能孔子所謂政猛於虎此其人也執事以
為日急誠急矣茲欲返之古也何繇哉亦
起其弊以維其風而已蓋士習之漓非
□□風之會起之也風之所尚在此孰

之工藝文者富靡麗之虛詞其流入于文
===

其人也執事以爲日漓誠漓矣以吏治言

□返其弊以維其風而巳蓋士習之漓非
□風之會起之也風之所尚在此孰
punctuated:
信也。然專任刑罰，而終抵罪誅，視康廉德讓之風，有餘愧焉。其不載之循吏者，固非無見也。以能著於東京者，若邊鳳、延篤之儔，非不卓然稱能也。然比迹趙、張，而政多深刻，視道德齊禮之治，有不逮焉。其不載之循吏者，曄非無見也。然則三代而下，語吏治之近古者，惟漢其庶幾乎！
至於今之士習吏治，則誠有可太息者焉。以士習言之，工藝文者，富靡麗之虛詞，其流入于支蔓而無實；談性命者，拾良知之餘緒，其究入於禪伯而無歸。孔子所謂「言有枝葉」，此其人也。執事以為日漓，誠漓矣。以吏治言之，習理財者，牟利秋毫，以督租辦課為有用；立刑威者，用刑次骨，以搏姦擊彊為已能。孔子所謂「政猛於虎」，此其人也。執事以為日急，誠急矣。
茲欲返之古也，何繇哉？亦起其弊，以維其風而已。蓋士習之漓，非□□風之會起之也。風之所尚在此，孰
translation_en:
…held in esteem and trusted. Yet they relied exclusively on punishments and ultimately incurred criminal penalties and execution. Measured against the ethos of peace, integrity, virtue, and deference, they had ample cause for shame. Their exclusion from the biographies of exemplary officials was certainly not without insight. Among those renowned for ability under the Eastern Han were men such as Bian Feng and Yan Du. They were indeed acclaimed for outstanding ability. Yet they followed in the footsteps of Zhao Guanghan and Zhang Chang, and their administration was often harsh and exacting. They fell short of government that guides through virtue and brings order through ritual. Ye [Fan Ye] was not without insight in excluding them from the biographies of exemplary officials. Thus, among the dynasties since the Three Dynasties, was it perhaps the Han alone whose administration approached that of antiquity?
As for the habits of scholars and the administration of officials today, there is indeed much to lament deeply. To speak of scholarly habits: those skilled in literary composition abound in ornate but empty phrases, drifting into rambling elaboration without substance; those who discuss human nature and destiny pick up leftover threads of teachings on innate moral knowledge, ultimately straying into the realm of Chan masters [?] without reaching any sound conclusion. These are the people Confucius meant when he spoke of “words with branches and leaves.” You say that their habits grow more debased by the day; debased they truly are. To speak of official administration: those practiced in managing finances seek profit down to the tiniest fraction, regarding the collection of land taxes and other revenues as useful service; those who establish their authority through punishment apply penalties that cut to the bone, regarding the suppression of evildoers and the powerful as proof of their own ability. These are the people to whom Confucius’s saying, “Government is fiercer than a tiger,” applies. You say that administration grows harsher by the day; harsh it truly is.
Now, if we wish to restore the ways of antiquity, by what means can we do so? Only by addressing these abuses and sustaining proper customs. For the deterioration of scholarly habits is not □□; prevailing fashions have brought it about [?]. When this is what prevailing custom esteems, who …

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不靡然從之耶誠能反其所尚求篤實之
士而工虛詞者弗庸則靡麗之風自息矣
求尚行之士而倡游言者勿聽則清談之
風自息矣孔子之誅正卯也以偽而辯孟
子論正人心也在放淫辭此非端士習之
一機乎如是而不返於淳者未之有也吏
治之急非自急也風之會起之也風之所
趨在此孰不羣然赴之耶誠能反其所趨
求仁愛之吏而巧為陰奪者必懲則聚斂
===
之風自息矣求平恕之吏而好為文致者
必譴則刻深之風自息矣尹鐸之治晉陽
也不為繭絲仇覽之論鷹鸇也不若鸞鳳
此非復吏治之一機乎如是而不返於古
者未之有也愚生才不足以經時學不足
以待問姑撫所見以復於執事者如此幸
進而教之
第三問
莊允中

不靡然從之耶誠能反其所尚□□□之
士而工虛詞者弗庸則靡麗之風自息矣
求尚行之士而倡游言者勿聽則淸談之
風自息矣孔子之誅正卯也以僞而辯孟
子論正人心也在放淫辭此非端士習之
一機乎如是而不返於淳者未之有也吏
治之急非自急也風之會起之也風之所
趨在此孰不羣然赴之耶誠能反其所趨
求仁愛之吏而巧爲陰奪者必懲則聚歛
===
之風自息矣求平恕之吏而好爲文致者
必譴則刻深之風自息矣尹鐸之治晉陽
也不爲繭絲仇覽之論鷹鸇也不若鸞鳳
此非復吏治之一機乎如是而不返於古
者未之有也愚生才不足以經時學不足
以待問姑撫所見以復於執事者如此幸
進而敎之
第三問
莊允中
punctuated:
不靡然從之耶？誠能反其所尚，求篤實之士而工虛詞者弗庸，則靡麗之風自息矣；求尚行之士而倡游言者勿聽，則清談之風自息矣。孔子之誅正卯也，以偽而辯；孟子論正人心也，在放淫辭。此非端士習之一機乎？如是而不返於淳者，未之有也。
吏治之急，非自急也，風之會起之也。風之所趨在此，孰不羣然赴之耶？誠能反其所趨，求仁愛之吏而巧為陰奪者必懲，則聚斂之風自息矣；求平恕之吏而好為文致者必譴，則刻深之風自息矣。尹鐸之治晉陽也，不為繭絲；仇覽之論鷹鸇也，不若鸞鳳。此非復吏治之一機乎？如是而不返於古者，未之有也。
愚生才不足以經時，學不足以待問，姑撫所見以復於執事者如此，幸進而教之。
第三問
莊允中
translation_en:
…would not yield to the prevailing fashion and follow it? If we could truly reverse what is esteemed, seek men of earnest integrity, and refuse to employ those skilled in empty rhetoric, the fashion for ornate extravagance would cease of itself. If we sought men who esteem practical conduct and refused to listen to those who promote idle talk, the fashion for empty discourse would cease of itself. Confucius executed Zhengmao because he was deceitful yet eloquent; when Mencius discussed rectifying people’s hearts, he emphasized banishing licentious speech. Is this not one means of correcting the habits of scholars? With such measures, there has never been a failure to return to sincerity and simplicity.
The harshness of official administration does not arise of itself: prevailing fashions bring it about. When fashion tends in this direction, who does not rush toward it with the crowd? If we could truly reverse this tendency, seek benevolent officials, and invariably punish those who cunningly despoil people in secret, the fashion for rapacious exaction would cease of itself. If we sought fair and forbearing officials and invariably censured those fond of fabricating charges, the fashion for cruel severity would cease of itself. When Yin Duo governed Jinyang, he did not treat its people as cocoons from which to reel silk. When Qiu Lan spoke of hawks and falcons, he judged them inferior to luan birds and phoenixes—that is, officials who govern through virtue rather than severity. Is this not one means of restoring proper administration? With such measures, there has never been a failure to return to the ways of antiquity.
My humble talents are insufficient to manage the affairs of the age, and my learning insufficient to answer your inquiries. Tentatively drawing upon what I have observed [?], I offer this reply to you. I hope you will grant me further instruction.
Third Question
Zhuang Yunzhong

text:
同考試官教諭陳批此策以道立意深得儒者
言行之要爲己之實且考據精詳議論宏博末復以發端極致爲
言尤見趨向之正若子可謂真儒矣
同考試官進士陳批篇中於六子言行撮舉不
遺評品允當且欲人師法孔子不爲賤儒深得程子立論之意其殆淹
貫經史而深有得者耶
考試官右中允張批博學詳說而能反說約焉是嘗
從事于爲己之學者取之
考試官右諭德丁批六子言行此策鋪叙有倫末復
折衷孔子其知所以入道而近儒者耶取之
===
儒者之學其必有準乎曰準乎道而已道
者學之鵠也射者弓矢誠習而不志於鵠
焉雖貫革不貴矣道者學之規也輿人輪
轅徒飾而不中乎規焉以致遠恐泥矣故
君子苞弁六藝矢聖陳謨非以譁衆也疆
理名物總挈治紀非以樹聲也緯緝經傳
疏通結滯非以徇象也矜慎容辭奧觀深
造非以干祿也專門守師窮智究慮非以

儒者之學，其必有準乎？曰：準乎道而已。道者，學之鵠也。射者弓矢誠習，而不志於鵠焉，雖貫革，不貴矣。道者，學之規也。輿人輪轅徒飾，而不中乎規焉，以致遠，恐泥矣。故君子苞弁六藝，矢聖陳謨，非以譁衆也；疆理名物，總挈治紀，非以樹聲也；緯緝經傳，疏通結滯，非以徇象也；矜慎容辭，奧觀深造，非以干祿也；專門守師，窮智究慮，非以
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Chen, an Instructor, comments: “This policy essay takes the Way as its central conception. It profoundly grasps the essentials of a Confucian scholar’s words and conduct and the substance of learning for one’s own cultivation. Its examination of sources is precise and thorough, and its arguments are broad and comprehensive. At the end it returns to the starting point and ultimate attainment, making especially clear the correctness of its orientation. Someone like you may indeed be called a true Confucian scholar.”

Associate Examiner Chen, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “The essay selects and presents the words and conduct of the six masters without omission, and its assessments are fair and fitting. Moreover, it urges people to take Confucius as their teacher and model, rather than become base Confucian scholars, profoundly grasping Master Cheng’s intention in advancing his argument. Might its author be someone thoroughly versed in the classics and histories who has attained deep understanding?”

Examiner Zhang, Right Companion, comments: “Broad in learning and detailed in exposition, he can nevertheless return to a concise statement of essentials. This is someone who has engaged in learning for his own cultivation. Accept him.”

Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher, comments: “This policy essay sets out the words and conduct of the six masters in orderly fashion, and concludes by taking Confucius as the standard of judgment. Does its author understand how to enter the Way and approach the standing of a Confucian scholar? Accept him.”

Must the learning of Confucian scholars have a standard? I say: its standard is simply the Way. The Way is the target of learning. If an archer is indeed practiced with bow and arrows but does not aim at the target, even piercing leather is of no value. The Way is the compass of learning. If a carriage maker merely embellishes the wheels and shafts without conforming to the compass, I fear that his carriage will become bogged down when used to travel far. Thus the gentleman comprehensively orders the Six Arts [?], takes the sages as his aim, and sets forth counsels—not to clamour for an audience’s attention; he delineates named categories and things and grasps the governing principles of administration—not to establish a reputation; he weaves together the classics and their commentaries and resolves tangled and obstructed passages—not to pursue outward forms [?]; he is circumspect in bearing and speech, probes mysteries, and pursues profound understanding—not to seek official emoluments; he devotes himself to a particular scholarly tradition and adheres to his teacher, exhausting his intelligence and deliberating to the utmost—not in order to …

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
自蔽也攬今撮古廣游逖覽非以眩博也
凡皆以爲道焉爾是故言以明道斯言爲
謨訓矣而識鑒之通蔽殊焉故言之合於
道者希也行以體道則行爲楷模矣而造
詣之深淺殊焉故行之合於道者希也以
其言道之難而人之言有幾於道焉則君
子取之不暇顧其餘言矣以其行道之難
而人之行有幾於道焉則君子取之不暇
責其餘行矣嗚呼此程子所以於六子有
===
取爾也且儒者之道非苟爲大而已性命
道德之奥具於心而天地萬物之理備於
我謏聞寡識不足以達觀蕩檢踰節不可
以盡性蓋昔孔子之述儒行有曰博學而
不窮篤行而不倦可謂一言以蔽之矣然
其博也將廣聞見以明吾之道而非汗漫
也其篤也將實踐履以行吾之道而非矯
拂也故曰君子儒爲已此子程子實見之
言也而乃有取於六子者非謂六子能爲

言也而乃有取於六子者非謂六子能爲
punctuated:
自蔽也。攬今撮古，廣游逖覽，非以眩博也。凡皆以爲道焉爾。是故言以明道，斯言爲謨訓矣，而識鑒之通蔽殊焉，故言之合於道者希也。行以體道，則行爲楷模矣，而造詣之深淺殊焉，故行之合於道者希也。以其言道之難，而人之言有幾於道焉，則君子取之，不暇顧其餘言矣。以其行道之難，而人之行有幾於道焉，則君子取之，不暇責其餘行矣。嗚呼！此程子所以於六子有取爾也。
且儒者之道，非苟爲大而已。性命道德之奥具於心，而天地萬物之理備於我。謏聞寡識，不足以達觀；蕩檢踰節，不可以盡性。蓋昔孔子之述儒行，有曰：「博學而不窮，篤行而不倦。」可謂一言以蔽之矣。然其博也，將廣聞見以明吾之道，而非汗漫也；其篤也，將實踐履以行吾之道，而非矯拂也。故曰：「君子儒爲已。」此子程子實見之言也。而乃有取於六子者，非謂六子能爲
translation_en:
…not to shut themselves off. They survey the present and gather from antiquity, travel widely and look far afield, not to dazzle others with their erudition. All these pursuits are simply for the sake of the Way. Thus, when words illuminate the Way, they become counsels and admonitions. Yet people differ in the clarity or obscurity of their understanding and discernment, so words that accord with the Way are rare. When conduct embodies the Way, it becomes an exemplary model. Yet people differ in the depth of their attainments, so conduct that accords with the Way is rare. Because speaking of the Way is difficult, whenever someone’s words approach it, the gentleman accepts them, without pausing to consider that person’s other words. Because practicing the Way is difficult, whenever someone’s conduct approaches it, the gentleman accepts it, without pausing to reproach that person’s other conduct. Ah! This is why Master Cheng found something to accept in the six thinkers.
Moreover, the Way of the Confucian scholar does not consist merely in striving for greatness. The mysteries of human nature, destiny, the Way, and virtue are present in the heart, and the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are fully contained within oneself. Scant learning and limited knowledge cannot yield comprehensive understanding; casting off restraints and overstepping proper bounds cannot fulfill one’s nature. When Confucius formerly described the conduct of Confucian scholars, he said: “They learn broadly without end and practice earnestly without weariness.” This may be said to sum it up in a single statement. Yet their breadth consists in extending what they hear and see in order to illuminate their own Way, rather than wandering without bounds; their earnestness consists in putting it into actual practice in order to carry out their own Way, rather than acting with strained contrariness. Hence the saying: “The gentlemanly Confucian scholar learns for his own sake.” This is a statement grounded in Master Cheng’s genuine insight. That he nevertheless found something to accept in the six thinkers does not mean that the six thinkers were able to…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
已也示爲已者以取人修學準也愚嘗反
覆往籍熟觀六子者之言與行而得其槩
矣蓋程子謂循其言可以入道者就三子
之言而取之也今觀管子之書有經言區
言短語雜篇輕重之別司馬遷嘗嘆其言
之詳矣夫其謹政通商均役盡利固莫非
富疆術者而乃有心術白心諸篇其言亦
出入吾儒誠正老子道德之間不悉中理
要然而有格言焉其心術下篇曰專於意
===
一於心思之思之不得鬼神教之非鬼神
之力也其精氣之極也茲其旨不與孔子
慎思之訓相發明與荀子之書有勸學修
身儒效王制等篇班固蓋謂之潤色孔子
之業矣夫其立言指事撥亂興理固莫非
翼六經者而乃有非十二子性惡諸篇其
中僞禮上霸至以子思孟子與墨翟惠施
同詆然而亦有格言焉其勸學篇曰其義
則始乎爲士終乎爲聖人真積力久則入

translation_en:
…for themselves; rather, he was showing those who learn for their own sake a standard for drawing upon others and cultivating their learning. I have repeatedly examined earlier writings, closely considering the words and conduct of these six masters, and have grasped their general character. When Master Cheng said that one could enter the Way by following their words, he was selecting what was valuable in the words of three of these masters.

Now, the Guanzi is divided into Canonical Sayings, Discourses on Particular Matters, Short Sayings, Miscellaneous Chapters, and Light and Heavy. Sima Qian once admired the thoroughness of its discussions. Its teachings on attending carefully to government, facilitating commerce, equalizing labor obligations, and fully realizing economic benefits are all techniques for enriching and strengthening the state. Yet it also contains chapters such as Techniques of the Mind and Purifying the Mind, whose teachings range between our Confucian doctrines of sincerity and rectification and Laozi’s doctrines of the Way and virtue. They do not all accord with the essentials of principle, but they nevertheless contain exemplary sayings. The lower chapter of Techniques of the Mind says: “Concentrate your intent and unify your mind. Think upon it, think upon it; if you cannot attain it, ghosts and spirits will teach you. This is not the power of ghosts and spirits: it is the utmost attainment of your vital essence.” Does the meaning of this passage not illuminate, and receive illumination from, Confucius’s injunction to think carefully?

The Xunzi contains chapters such as Encouraging Learning, Cultivating Oneself, The Achievements of the Confucians, and Royal Institutions. Ban Gu indeed described it as embellishing the work of Confucius. Its formulation of teachings and discussion of affairs, its overcoming of disorder and promotion of good order, all support the Six Classics. Yet it also contains chapters such as Against the Twelve Masters and Human Nature Is Evil. In these it treats ritual as artificial and esteems hegemony [?], even condemning Zisi and Mengzi together with Mo Di and Hui Shi. Nevertheless, it too contains exemplary sayings. Its chapter Encouraging Learning says: “As to its meaning, it begins with becoming a scholar and ends with becoming a sage. Through genuine accumulation and prolonged effort, one enters…”

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
學至乎沒而後止也玆其詞不與說命典
學之言相表裏與若夫杜預之爲春秋經
傳集解也大觀羣典簡公羊穀梁詭辯之
言錯綜微辭備劉賈許穎異同之致世以
爲丘明忠臣信矣然而棄經信傳鴻生致
譏發明雖多間失本意則由其遜德罔企
庶幾立言武庫流稱自占傳癖云爾然其
叙傳有曰優而游之使自求之厭而飫之
使自趨之若江海之浸膏澤之潤渙然氷
釋怡然理順此與孟子深造自得之㫖又
何相遠乎此三言者固程子所取也夫以
三子著述之富若彼而可循之以入道者
僅僅若此則其言之不足取者多矣明道
豈易耶程子謂近似儒者氣象就三子之
行而取之也今考仲舒進退容止非禮不
行兩相驕王正色率下天人相與之策明

…learning ceases only at death.” Do these words not complement the injunction to constant study in the “Charge to Yue” (Yue ming)? As for Du Yu’s Collected Explanations of the Classic and Commentary of the Spring and Autumn Annals, he surveyed the canonical writings extensively, sifted out the specious arguments of the Gongyang and Guliang commentaries, interwove the subtle expressions, and fully set forth the points of agreement and disagreement among Liu, Jia, Xu, and Ying. The world regarded him as Qiuming’s loyal minister, and rightly so. Yet eminent scholars criticized him for abandoning the Classic and trusting the Commentary. Although he elucidated much, he sometimes missed the original meaning. This was because, yielding precedence in virtue, he did not aspire to it [?], but hoped to establish a lasting legacy through his writings. He acquired the sobriquet “Arsenal” and professed himself addicted to the Commentary—that was all. Yet his preface to the Commentary says: “Let them roam at ease, so that they seek it for themselves; let them have their fill, so that they advance toward it of themselves. Like immersion in rivers and seas, like the moistening of nourishing rain, the ice dissolves completely, and the principles fall smoothly into place.” How far is this from Mencius’s teaching of profound attainment and making understanding one’s own? These three sayings were indeed what Master Cheng approved. Given the abundance of these three thinkers’ writings, if so little could be followed as a means of entering the Way, then much of what they said was unworthy of acceptance. How could illuminating the Way be easy? When Master Cheng said that they approached the bearing of a Confucian, he was approving aspects of their conduct.

Now, examining Dong Zhongshu, we find that in his movements and bearing he did nothing contrary to ritual propriety. Twice serving as chancellor to arrogant princes, he maintained a grave demeanor and led his subordinates by example. His policy essays on the interaction of Heaven and humanity clarified the foundations of human nature and the methods of its cultivation; his counsels on rectifying righteousness and illuminating the Way distinguished the intentions and deeds of true kings from those of hegemons. As for such teachings as his doctrine of grand unity and his doctrine of relying on virtue rather than punishments, indeed …

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
自孟子而後世未有言之粹然一出於正
如此者則其造詣之正可知矣雖其生質
天命人欲之分未極根柢乃其學問小疵
真氏謂得從游聖門當無慙游夏者不亦
度粤諸子也與揚子雲博覽好學不為章
句簡易清靜不修廉隅慮小辯之破大道
則為法言以祛惑推大運以思渾天則為
太玄經以衍數它如訓纂之作州箴之作
博物洽聞其言有補於世則其造詣之深
===
可知矣至於信在黃宮靈根内美之測乃
其地位所至桓譚謂文義至深而論不詭
於聖人此漢儒中必以為賢也與大毛公
之為詩傳也明四始以正經本分小序以
冠篇端析義也精河間獻王取之而晁氏
稱其密措辭也簡劉孝孫則之而李邦直
賛其深源流於子夏仲梁子最為授受之
正考証於先秦古文多合盡洗三氏之非
嘗觀漢藝文志載諸儒解經有五字用三

punctuated: 自孟子而後，世未有言之粹然一出於正如此者，則其造詣之正可知矣。雖其生質、天命、人欲之分未極根柢，乃其學問小疵。真氏謂得從游聖門，當無慙游夏者，不亦度粤諸子也與？揚子雲博覽好學，不為章句，簡易清靜，不修廉隅。慮小辯之破大道，則為《法言》以祛惑；推大運以思渾天，則為《太玄經》以衍數。它如《訓纂》之作、《州箴》之作，博物洽聞，其言有補於世，則其造詣之深可知矣。至於信在黃宮、靈根内美之測，乃其地位所至。桓譚謂文義至深，而論不詭於聖人，此漢儒中必以為賢也與？大毛公之為《詩傳》也，明四始以正經本，分小序以冠篇端。析義也精，河間獻王取之，而晁氏稱其密；措辭也簡，劉孝孫則之，而李邦直賛其深。源流於子夏、仲梁子，最為授受之正；考証於先秦古文，多合，盡洗三氏之非。嘗觀《漢藝文志》載諸儒解經，有五字用三
translation_en:
…since Mengzi, the world has known no one whose words were so pure and issued so entirely from what is right. From this we can recognize the soundness of his attainment. Although his distinctions among inborn constitution, Heaven’s mandate, and human desires did not reach their very roots, these were minor flaws in his learning. Master Zhen said that, had he been able to study in the Sage’s school, he would have had no cause for shame before Ziyou and Zixia. Did he not surpass the other masters [?]?

Yang Ziyun read widely and loved learning, without devoting himself to textual divisions and explanations of individual phrases. Simple, unassuming, tranquil, and quiet, he did not cultivate an ostentatiously rigid rectitude. Concerned that petty disputations would undermine the Great Way, he wrote Model Sayings (Fayan) to dispel confusion. Investigating the great cosmic revolutions and reflecting on the spherical heavens, he wrote the Classic of the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan jing) to elaborate numerical principles. Other works, such as his Compilation of Explanations (Xunzuan) and Admonitions to the Provinces (Zhouzhen), display extensive knowledge and learning. His words benefited the world, showing the depth of his attainment. As for the interpretive statements concerning “trust residing in the Yellow Palace” and “the numinous root’s inner beauty,” these expressed the level he had reached. Huan Tan said that his writings were profoundly meaningful and that his arguments did not depart from the sages. Surely he must be counted among the worthy scholars of the Han?

When the Elder Master Mao composed his Commentary on the Odes, he clarified the Four Beginnings to establish the foundations of the classic and set out the Lesser Prefaces at the head of the individual poems. His analysis of meaning was precise: Prince Xian of Hejian adopted it, and Master Chao praised its meticulousness. His wording was concise: Liu Xiaosun took it as his model, and Li Bangzhi praised its depth. Its lineage derived from Zixia and Zhongliangzi, giving it a particularly sound transmission from teacher to pupil. When checked against ancient writings from before the Qin, it agreed in many instances, thoroughly clearing away the errors of the three other schools. I once read in the Treatise on Literature in the History of the Han that, among the scholars who explained the classics, there were some who, in explaining five characters, used three…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
萬言者其漫漶若爾故程子曰漢儒談經
不知要唯大毛公有儒者氣象又曰毛萇
最得聖賢之意得非因其訓詁而覘其造
詣乎夫以漢世經學之專如彼而氣象之
近儒者僅僅若此則其人之不足取者多
矣體道豈易耶抑程子有取於三子之言
矣復曰三子初不及此有取於三子之行
矣而乃曰近似是皆猶有所未滿者無亦
抗道之大高而責人之甚備與蓋有說矣
===
儒者於道求以明諸心故學不可不好也
博依之以貫其類深思之以凝其精厚積
之以俟於化庶道之能明耳三子言之宜
所造之及此矣而程子不許者則以杜之
博依徒牽通乎義數管之精思亦役志於
權謀荀之真積又徇心於執見蓋其言雖
是而所以從事則與道固遠耳儒者於道
求以體諸身故行不可不力也道德求其
和順焉理義求其浹洽焉涵養求其深沉

矣而乃曰近似是皆猶有所未滿者無亦
杭道之大高而責人之甚備與蓋有說矣
===
儒者於道求以明諸心故學不可不好也
博依之以貫其類深思之以纘其精厚積
之以俟於化庶道之能明耳三子言之宜

權謀苟之真積又狥心於執見蓋其言雖
是而所以從事則與道固遠耳儒者於道
求以體諸身故行不可不力也道德求其
和順焉理義求其浹洽焉涵養求其深沉
punctuated:
萬言者，其漫漶若爾。故程子曰：「漢儒談經不知要，唯大毛公有儒者氣象。」又曰：「毛萇最得聖賢之意。」得非因其訓詁而覘其造詣乎？夫以漢世經學之專如彼，而氣象之近儒者僅僅若此，則其人之不足取者多矣。體道豈易耶？抑程子有取於三子之言矣，復曰：「三子初不及此。」有取於三子之行矣，而乃曰：「近似。」是皆猶有所未滿者，無亦抗道之大高，而責人之甚備與？蓋有說矣。

儒者於道，求以明諸心，故學不可不好也。博依之以貫其類，深思之以凝其精，厚積之以俟於化，庶道之能明耳。三子言之，宜所造之及此矣，而程子不許者，則以杜之博依徒牽通乎義數，管之精思亦役志於權謀，荀之真積又徇心於執見。蓋其言雖是，而所以從事則與道固遠耳。儒者於道，求以體諸身，故行不可不力也。道德求其和順焉，理義求其浹洽焉，涵養求其深沉
translation_en:
…thousand words: such was their diffuseness and obscurity. Thus Master Cheng said, “When Han scholars discussed the classics, they did not grasp the essentials; only the Elder Master Mao had the bearing of a true Confucian scholar.” He also said, “Mao Chang best grasped the intentions of the sages and worthies.” Was it not through Mao’s explanations of words that he discerned the level of his attainment? If, despite such specialized study of the classics in the Han, so few scholars even approached the bearing of a true Confucian, then many must have fallen short of deserving approval. How could embodying the Way be easy? Yet Master Cheng approved of the words of the three masters, only to say again, “The three masters never attained this.” He approved of the conduct of another three masters, yet said only that it “closely resembled” the ideal. In all these cases he still found something wanting. Was he perhaps setting the Way too high and demanding too much perfection of others? There is, however, an explanation.

In relation to the Way, Confucian scholars seek to understand it clearly in their hearts; hence they must love learning. They draw broadly on sources to comprehend connected categories, reflect deeply to concentrate their essential understanding, and build up substantial learning while awaiting transformation: only thus may they hope to understand the Way clearly. From what the three masters said, one might suppose that their attainments had reached this level. Yet Master Cheng withheld his approval because Du’s broad recourse to sources merely forced connections among meanings and numerical schemes; Guan’s concentrated thought likewise put his mind in the service of expedient stratagems; and Xun’s genuine accumulation of effort also indulged his attachment to fixed opinions. Although their words were correct, the way they put them into practice was far indeed from the Way. In relation to the Way, Confucian scholars seek to embody it in their own persons; hence they must exert themselves in practice. In the Way and virtue they seek harmony and accord; in principle and righteousness they seek thorough assimilation; in nurturing their character they seek depth and composure…

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
焉庶道之能行焉耳三子行之即名之曰
儒亦奚不可而程子靳之者則以董之經
術正矣而有陰陽之溺揚之搆擬深矣而
失節義之經毛之釋義精矣而又無可見
之行蓋其質雖美而終身所至尚未得所
安耳學者誠能循三子之言而得其學之
所發端由三子之造而進於學之所極致
則道德性命之奥天地萬物之理皆將一
以貫之而所謂魯國之儒一人者固吾師
===
也於六子何有哉不然馳騁口耳博學爲
務外耳子張氏之賤儒也拘牽儀度篤行
爲狥迹耳子夏氏之賤儒也豈程子示人
爲己意耶謹對
第四問
高文炳
同考試官教諭魯 批 當天下難處之事而能臨
機決策足以定國是而銷奸萌則卓識神敏英斷三者缺一不可是作
根極理要敷析詳明精練之才弘濟之猷可以具見錄之

同考試官教諭魯　批〔當天下難處之事而能臨〕
〔機決策足以定國是而銷奸萌則非識神敏莫斷二者缺一不可是作〕
〔根極理要剖析詳明精練之才弘濟之猷可以具見錄之〕
punctuated:
焉，庶道之能行焉耳。三子行之，即名之曰儒，亦奚不可？而程子靳之者，則以董之經術正矣，而有陰陽之溺；揚之搆擬深矣，而失節義之經；毛之釋義精矣，而又無可見之行。蓋其質雖美，而終身所至，尚未得所安耳。學者誠能循三子之言，而得其學之所發端；由三子之造，而進於學之所極致，則道德性命之奥、天地萬物之理，皆將一以貫之。而所謂魯國之儒一人者，固吾師也，於六子何有哉？不然，馳騁口耳，博學爲務外耳，子張氏之賤儒也；拘牽儀度，篤行爲狥迹耳，子夏氏之賤儒也。豈程子示人爲己意耶？謹對。

第四問
高文炳

同考試官教諭魯批：當天下難處之事，而能臨機決策，足以定國是而銷奸萌，則卓識、神敏、英斷三者缺一不可。是作根極理要，敷析詳明，精練之才、弘濟之猷，可以具見，錄之。
translation_en:
…Only then may one hope to put the Way into practice. Given the conduct of these three masters, what would be wrong with calling them Confucian scholars? Yet Master Cheng withheld that designation because, although Dong’s classical learning was sound, he became immersed in yin and yang; although Yang’s constructions and imitations were profound, he departed from the constant standards of integrity and righteousness; and although Mao’s explanations of meaning were refined, he had no demonstrable conduct to his credit. Although their native qualities were admirable, their lifelong attainments had not yet brought them to a secure resting place.

If students can truly follow the words of the three masters and grasp the starting point of their learning, and proceed from the attainments of the other three toward learning’s ultimate achievement, then the mysteries of the Way, virtue, human nature, and destiny, and the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things, will all be united by a single thread. The so-called sole Confucian scholar in the state of Lu is assuredly my teacher. What need, then, have I of these six masters? Otherwise, merely ranging over what enters the ears and leaves the mouth makes extensive learning a pursuit of externals—the debased Confucianism of Zizhang’s school. Being constrained by ceremonial forms and prescribed measures makes earnest practice merely a pursuit of outward traces—the debased Confucianism of Zixia’s school. Could this be Master Cheng’s intention in teaching people to learn for their own moral cultivation? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fourth Question
Gao Wenbing

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Instructor: When confronting affairs that are difficult to manage in the realm, one must be able to decide upon a course of action as circumstances arise, sufficiently to settle the direction of state policy and extinguish treachery at its inception. Outstanding discernment, extraordinary quickness of mind, and resolute judgment are all indispensable. This composition probes the essential principles to their roots and expounds and analyzes them clearly and thoroughly. Both accomplished ability and plans for rendering far-reaching service are fully evident. Selected for inclusion.

title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官進士邵批士君子於古人行事妙處
當設身處地然後智慮精明臨事亦可比迹往哲此作以六子所處探
究本原歸之識與敏斷而度勢觀變審幾尤盡事情曲折至末二喻且
親切確當可以觀子之才識過人遠矣大受之器非子其誰敬服敬服
考試官右中允張批察微應卒古人識度有不可測
者子能抵掌談之亦負竒之士哉
考試官右諭德丁批古人善處大事類非後人所及子
能一言之是可大受者敬服敬服
君子之於天下也以審勢者尚其識以應
變者尚其敏以裁幾者尚其斷何則天下
之事其成敗相歭輕重之懸於低昻者所
謂勢也其情偽相感利害之判於呼吸者
所謂變也其愛惡相攻是非之淆於糾結

Only then will his understanding and deliberation become keen and clear, enabling him, when confronting affairs, to match the achievements of earlier worthies. This essay investigates fundamental principles through the situations faced by the six masters, attributing their success to discernment, quickness, and resolution. Its assessment of circumstances, observation of changes, and scrutiny of incipient developments bring out especially well all the intricacies of affairs. The final two analogies are also apt and precise. This shows how far your talent and discernment surpass those of others. Who but you is fitted to bear great responsibilities? I admire you! I admire you!

Comment by Examiner Ding, Right Admonisher: The ancients’ skill in handling great affairs was generally beyond the reach of later men. You can express this in a single statement; you are someone capable of bearing great responsibilities. I admire you! I admire you!

In dealing with the affairs of the world, a gentleman prizes discernment for assessing circumstances, quickness for responding to changes, and resolution for deciding at the first signs of developments. Why is this? In worldly affairs, where success and failure stand opposed [?], and the balance of importance hangs upon a rise or fall—this is what is meant by circumstances. Where sincerity and deception act upon one another, and benefit and harm are decided in the space of a breath—this is what is meant by change. title: 隆慶元年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之人所以大過人者不以是哉明問及此
固愚生就正之地也敢不尋繹以對人之
言曰我善論事不知論事非難處事為難
也人之言曰我善處事不知處事固難處
危疑反側之事尤難也何也事無常形難
以一執以成敗言有垂成而敗者有因敗
為功者有不密害成者有敬慎不敗者其
勢不可常也以利害言有似利而實害者
有不以利為利者有利害相當者有利多
===
害少者其變不可窮也以是非言有人以
為是而已以為非者有人以為非而已以
為是者有是而疑於非非而疑於是者其
幾不可測也是皆不可以不察也嗚呼非
有過人之識先覺之敏毅然之斷其孰能
善處之哉愚嘗上下古今得聞其槩矣漢
室之初諸侯强大緩之則相習驕奢易為
淫亂急之則阻强合從以逆京師天下之
憂未有大於此者也時有建分王子弟之

translation_en:
…Was it not through these qualities that the men of antiquity so greatly surpassed others? Your enlightened question touches on this very matter, giving an ignorant student such as myself an opportunity to seek correction. How could I fail to examine it closely and reply?

People say, “I am good at discussing affairs,” without understanding that discussing affairs is not difficult; managing them is difficult. People say, “I am good at managing affairs,” without understanding that, difficult as managing affairs certainly is, managing affairs fraught with danger, uncertainty, and unrest is harder still. Why is this? Affairs have no fixed form and are difficult to handle by adhering to a single rule. In terms of success and failure, some fail on the verge of success; some turn failure into achievement; some spoil success through a lack of secrecy; and some avoid failure through reverent caution. The configuration of circumstances cannot remain constant. In terms of benefit and harm, some things appear beneficial but are actually harmful; some do not take apparent benefit to be true benefit; in some cases benefit and harm balance each other; and in others benefit outweighs harm. Their changes are inexhaustible. In terms of right and wrong, there are things others consider right but oneself considers wrong [?], and things others consider wrong but oneself considers right [?]; there are things that are right but seem wrong, and things that are wrong but seem right. Their subtle incipient tendencies cannot be fathomed. All these require careful scrutiny.

Alas! Without surpassing discernment, the acuity to perceive things before others, and resolute decisiveness, who could manage them well? I have surveyed antiquity and more recent times and have learned something of their broad outlines. At the beginning of the Han dynasty, the feudatory princes were powerful. If treated leniently, they would encourage one another in arrogance and extravagance and readily descend into excess and disorder; if pressed hard, they would rely on their strength and form alliances to defy the capital. No concern in the realm was greater than this. At that time, someone proposed dividing their territories and enfeoffing their sons and younger brothers…

text:
說而致諸侯尋弱如主父偃者是說也一
以宣仁孝之道一以銷逆節之萌所謂不
動聲色而措漢室於泰山之安者偃之力
居多矣吾不謂習縱橫之術如偃者其謀
及此也或者曰偃之策賈誼先發之矣豈
智謀之士所見畧同耶唐季之衰節鎮跋
扈無事則擁重柄以輕朝廷有事則倚強
藩而挾天子天下之患未有大於此者也
後有建收兵制賦之計而致節鎮遂銷如
===
趙普者是計也一以全君臣之恩一以息
兵革之禍所謂不動聲色而措天下於泰
山之安者普之謀誠善矣吾不謂多智之
學究如普者其計出此也或者曰普之策
烏重胤先發之矣豈獨見之言有所偶合
耶迺若德宗之世藩鎮拒命銳意除之諸
鎮憚其威嚴矣時淄青節度李正巳者表
獻錢三十萬此以辭受甞朝廷也德宗欲
受則恐爲所欺卻之則逆其來意此國是
